Discord Rewrites Desktop and Mobile Clients in Rust Using Zed's GPU-Accelerated Rendering Framework

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Discord Rewrites Desktop and Mobile Clients in Rust Using Zed's GPU-Accelerated Rendering Framework.
  • Nov 19, 2026 3 min read.
  • Discord’s CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy recently unveiled rewriting its desktop and mobile clients in Rust, moving away from Electron and React Native.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Discord Rewrites Desktop and Mobile Clients in Rust Using Zed's GPU-Accelerated Rendering Framework.

Nov 19, 2026 3 min read.

Discord’s CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy recently unveiled rewriting its desktop and mobile clients in Rust, moving away from Electron and React Native. The project (codenamed Phoenix) eliminates layers of abstraction to directly leverage the device’s GPU, native mobile views, and a Rust core shared across platforms. Early results hint at a significant reduction in RAM usage and boot time for chat, voice, and streaming.

Vishnevskiy expanded on the rewrite on X:.

It has been revealed that we’ve been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there. That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust. We hope to get it into testing with customers soon™. (And it’s not Tauri, it’s GPUI, so good guess everyone.).

According to recent reports, the desktop app thus drops Chromium/Node.js for GPUI, the open-source, GPU-accelerated Rust UI framework built by the Zed team for the Zed editor. Zed is an open-source code editor written in Rust for macOS, Linux, and Windows by a team including the creators of GitHub’s Atom code editor, which was sunsetted in 2022, four years after Microsoft’s acquisition of GitHub. Zed touts a narrow focus on performance and user (i.e., developer) experience:.

VS Code won by being good enough for everyone. Zed wins by being excellent for developers who refuse to compromise on speed.

Discord’s mobile app rewrite drops React Native, instead directly leveraging native iOS and Android views and reusing a common Rust core.

Industry observers note that the browser client keeps rendering HTML with the application logic layer compiled to WebAssembly. Embedded web surfaces (e.g., YouTube videos and Activities), however, invoke an OS webview, with Electron’s built-in browser no longer available.

Vishnevskiy signals decreasing RAM usage, startup time, and latency as key motivations behind the rewrite:.

The newly introduced Discord client using less RAM is just part of the story. Clicking around feels instant, I can’t go back. Check out the boot time.

Early internal builds for the desktop app reveal RAM usage at around 290 MB (measured with two accounts logged in simultaneously) and a near-instant cold start versus 5.5 s on Electron.

Vishnevskiy showcased similar improvements on mobile with a load time under 2 seconds for the rewrite versus approximately 5 seconds for the legacy app.

Elias Floreteng, in his master’s thesis at KTH this year (An Empirical Study of React Native’s Newly introduced Architecture), reported performance gains across several metrics for native Swift and Kotlin over React Native, even with its new architecture. The controlled benchmark involves a 1,000-row scrollable image list using stock list and image components, with identical assets and row geometry across all binaries. Floreteng concludes that Swift beats React Native across every comparable runtime metric on iOS. On Android, the gap to native is small and runs in both directions, with native ahead on memory and CPU.

On desktop, Zed proved that leveraging GPUI could provide better performance over Electron and alternative frameworks reusing the device’s native webview (e.g., Tauri).

Industry observers note that while Tauri also uses a Rust backend, it leverages the operating system’s native webview. This has the advantage of letting web developers reuse their knowledge of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, while also avoiding the bundling of Chromium. Executable size is, as a result, generally smaller. Tauri apps’ RAM usage on Windows, however, tends to be similar to that of their Electron counterparts, as the same core, resource-hungry browser technology is used. Webview behavior may also be inconsistent across operating systems.

GPUI replaces the browser engine with a hybrid immediate and retained mode, GPU-accelerated UI framework that targets 120-frames-per-second rendering without garbage-collection pauses. In exchange for the reported performance gains, developers give up many rendering and accessibility features that come baked into the browser (e.g., text layout, input method integration, screen-reader accessibility hooks, right-to-left support). While miscellaneous Rust libraries exist to address some of these issues (e.g., Parley for text layout), developers still have to wire them into a consistent user experience.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

NetWasm 0.10 Speeds Up C# on WebAssembly, Now Faster Than Mono AOT

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News NetWasm 0.10 Speeds Up C# on WebAssembly, Now Faster Than Mono AOT.
  • Nov 19, 2026 3 min read.
  • In a recent development, the team behind NetWasm has published a write-up of its 0.10 optimisation work, spanning releases 0.10.1 to 0.10.8.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News NetWasm 0.10 Speeds Up C# on WebAssembly, Now Faster Than Mono AOT.

Nov 19, 2026 3 min read.

In a recent development, the team behind NetWasm has published a write-up of its 0.10 optimisation work, spanning releases 0.10.1 to 0.10.8. The changes touch exception handling, array bounds checks, WebAssembly SIMD and integer division. On the project’s own benchmark set, NetWasm now comes out ahead of Mono AOT and gets close to desktop .NET on some workloads.

Sources indicate that netWasm is a compiler and runtime that compiles C# programs ahead of time into small, standalone WebAssembly files. It takes the IL that Roslyn produces and emits Wasm, using its own runtime and a CoreLib ported from .NET. The yardstick is the Mono AOT build for WASI, which runs .NET on the same engine. A fresh garbage collector had already put NetWasm in front on allocation-heavy code, but plain loops were still slower: a quicksort of 100,000 integers took 77.2 ms, against 58.0 ms for Mono AOT.

Much of the early gain came from exception handling in 0.10.1. Wasmtime adds extra register save-and-restore code around any function that can throw or catch, floating-point registers included. Methods with null, bounds or checked-arithmetic checks paid that price on every call. Throws now go through a shared function and the catching handler releases the frames, which cut UI churn from 17.6 to 7.9 ms.

Version 0.10.2 inlines small straight-line methods in loops, tuple swaps included, and skips checks already performed on the same array and index. The quicksort fell to 54.0 ms. DoomSharp, a C# software renderer for Doom that ships a NetWasm build, served as a second test case. Value-type accessors now compile to plain field loads, and at O3 small branching helpers are inlined inside loops. Together these brought a 120-frame render from 3,595 down to 1,934 ms.

In a recent development, SIMD arrived in 0.10.7. Vector128, Vector and PackedSimd lower to 128-bit Wasm instructions, and element-wise array loops handle four or more elements per iteration, with a scalar fallback. Hoisting loop-invariant Math calls allowed a solver for Burgers’ equation, a fundamental partial differential equation from fluid mechanics, to vectorise: its first test dropped from 497 ms to 71 ms, against 186 ms for Mono AOT and 93 ms for desktop .NET.

It has been revealed that version 0.10.8 targets division and range-checked arithmetic. A remainder that follows a division now reuses the quotient and skips repeated zero-divisor and int.MinValue / -1 checks. A trial-division test fell from 1,376 to 765 ms, while Mono AOT needed 862 ms.

It has been revealed that across the 2,213 cases, 0.10.8 at O3 with NetWasmGC takes 0.41 times Mono AOT’s time as a geometric mean, excluding five cases where Mono’s LLVM removes the work. Against desktop .NET 11 RC3 JIT the ratio is 0.87, down from 2.15 for 0.10.6. By family, the ratio to Mono AOT runs from 0.34 for intrinsics to 0.81 for math. The 120-frame DoomSharp render takes 1,623 ms on NetWasmGC, compared with 2,371 ms for Mono AOT and 1,053 ms for desktop .NET JIT.

Those figures come from Wasmtime 49.0.3 on an Apple M1 Max, using cases from dotnet/performance plus five NetWasm workloads. The authors also found that identical loops at different addresses could differ by up to 15 per cent, so their A/B tests align every function to 4 KiB.

The article is open about what is left. Desktop .NET is about 3.1 times faster on vector benchmarks, because it can use host SIMD directly while Wasm is limited to fixed 128-bit operations. Math.Pow is 1.4 times slower than on Mono AOT, and CopyBlock64 is 3.3 times slower. One workload, NewtR, regressed to 1.9 times slower than in 0.10.6, which the authors blame on Wasmtime’s register allocator keeping a value in a stack slot around the loop.

In a recent development, since the numbers are self-reported and come from one machine and one runtime, results elsewhere may differ. NetWasm can be tried in the online playground, and local setup is covered in the compile and publish guide. Developers can find the documentation is in the official GitHub repository.

Multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Seven vulnerabilities have been discovered in Ruby’s regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings.
  • CVE identifiers have been requested for these vulnerabilities but have not been assigned yet, so this advisory refers to them by their GitHub Security Advisory (GHSA) identifiers.
  • Ruby has a one-byte heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Seven vulnerabilities have been discovered in Ruby’s regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings. We are aware of PoCs that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution. We have released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 to fix them. We strongly recommend upgrading.

CVE identifiers have been requested for these vulnerabilities but have not been assigned yet, so this advisory refers to them by their GitHub Security Advisory (GHSA) identifiers.

Ruby has a one-byte heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

Recent findings suggest that ruby has a double free in its regular expression engine. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

Ruby has an integer overflow in the case conversion of strings, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

Sources indicate that ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching against a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that use attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can lead to memory corruption in an attacker-controlled way.

Industry observers note that ruby has an integer overflow in its regular expression engine, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

Industry observers note that ruby has a heap-based buffer overflow in Regexp#to_s. Converting a crafted regular expression to a string may allow information disclosure or remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching a crafted string may disclose memory contents or crash the process.

We strongly recommend upgrading to Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 or 3.3.14.

According to recent reports, ruby 3.3 is in the security maintenance phase. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached their end of life and will not receive these fixes.

Like I could do A/B tests, stuff like that. I think it's a real concern, and I don't think there's a great answer right now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the bug is reachable from the following frameworks in their default configuration. Other frameworks are not exposed by default, but application code that upcases strings received in a legacy encoding may also be vulnerable.

The latest version of the following popular software bundles an affected Ruby.

Updated 19 November 2026 at 15:29 UTC.

Upgrade Ruby to a fixed release: 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10.

Install the vendor's fixed release. See Self-hosted software for fixed versions of popular products.

Most of Ruby's single-byte encodings have no capital Ã. Upcasing it writes two bytes, SS, but the loop only bounds-checks one (to < to_end).

The output buffer is allocated as the input length plus 20 bytes. Each Ã adds one byte to the output, so an input with 21 of them overflows the buffer by one byte.

It has been revealed that the same loop is in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings and has been there since Ruby 2.4.0. It is reached by upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?.

UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.

Fixed upstream in ruby/ruby@d582f8f.

In a recent development, A one-byte heap overflow. The byte written is S (0x53) when upcasing or s (0x73) when case-folding, and it lands directly after the output buffer. The attacker controls the size of the buffer through the input length.

Copying the result out of the buffer then reads one byte out of bounds.

We'll be publishing a proof of concept in a week, once people have had time to upgrade.

15M web servers on one VM – smoltcp, DPDK, AF_XDP

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that put a web server online and everyone starts trying to hack it. Why? A basic rule of economics. Short supply, substantial demand - there arenât enough web servers for everyone. Letâs run a web server for every human on the planet, all 8 billion of them. I couldnât get funding, so weâre bootstrapping. The goal is to run 15 million web servers on one VM with 10GB of RAM and 1 CPU core. If we succeed, Iâll find some RAM from old microwaves around the house and weâll scale it up so everyone can have their own web server. Demand will drop to zero and cybersecurity will be solved once and for all.Web serverInstead of vibe coding it all, letâs use an ancient technique called learning. First of all, what is a web server? There are a few essential syscalls.listen - syscall, asks kernel to listen for connections on a socketaccept - syscall, accepts a connection on a socketrecv - receives data from a socketsend - sends dataclose - closesWhat is a syscall? A function that is executed by the OS kernel. Whatever fancy language or library you use for HTTP, it all comes down to those syscalls (well, yes, but actually no). Letâs use C to make it all explicit. We start listening, then read from the socket in a loop and always reply with OK.int main(void) { // We use port 0 which makes OS return any available port int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); if (listen(server, 128) < 0) return 1; const char reply[] = "HTTP/1.0 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nOK"; for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) { if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0) send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL); close(client); } }It couldnât be simpler: listen on a socket, accept a connection, read the data, send a reply, close the client connection, and repeat. It gives us around 65k RPS. Now that weâve learned everything, letâs finish the article and call it a day:$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server &; done ... ... 28232 program exited with error 1Hm, why did listen fail? Ah, weâve run out of ports! Weâre using port=0, so the kernel picks an available port from ip_local_port_range.$ sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768 60999Why are so many ports skipped? Historically, port 0 was created for outbound connections. When you call connect('example.com', 80), Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from ip_local_port_range to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small.Port 0 is special. You cannot listen on it (actually, you can - https://acid.vegas/blog/the-port-that-does-not-exist/).Ports 1-1024 require root.Ports 1024-32768 are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You donât want to call connect('example.com') and end up allocating port 3306 to receive incoming data. mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox would make for a confusing UX.Ports 60999 - 65535 are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading.Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using 1-65535, but thatâs still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware. Letâs simply connect 15M/32k=450 new network cards to the server.The 65k limit comes from the TCP standard. A port is a u16, so even if we hack the kernel with find '*.c' -exec sed -i 's/u16/u32/' \; to support bigger port numbers, normal clients still wouldnât be able to connect. Each listening server is identified by a (protocol, IP, port) tuple. That explains how we can use the same port for UDP and TCP. It also means we can use a bunch of different IPs for our web servers. If we connect 450 network cards to the server, weâll get 450 unique IP addresses and be able to listen on 15 million unique addresses!UPD. Iâve heard from readers that the network card is the ONLY hardware component that didnât get 100 times more expensive in the last year. Canât we avoid ruining that too and solve this in software?Letâs use a beautiful technology called AnyIP, which lets us listen on a whole subnet. Many VPS and dedicated server providers routinely give you a whole TCPv6 subnet. We can simply run sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo to get 18 quintillion addresses (plus or minus one) to listen on. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. Weâll change our server to pick the nth IP from our range:// Read IP index from CLI, shift base IP by it int i = read_cli_param(argv[1]); const uint32_t base_ip = 0x0a400001; // ex. 10.64.0.1 addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(first_ip + i); // shift, ex. 10.64.0.2And now we can finally finish the article.$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server $i &; done ... ... Out of memoryHm, one server consumes 1.5MB of RAM, so running that many would takeâ¦ 20TB of RAM, which is a few bytes more than our 10GB budget.RuntimeBy pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In Userland Linux scheduler in Rust, I revealed how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task.TLDR: Weâre using LFI for sandboxing. It gives us memory isolation and replaces all syscalls with calls to our host handler, which lets us implement I/O however we like. To schedule multiple guests, we load them all into our main processâs memory and make the CPU constantly switch between guests - we become our own micro OS.Since we need to save every byte and CPU cycle we can, weâre doomed to build another specialised runtime. Letâs get started. How much is 10GB divided by 15M, exactly?Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. Whatâs the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Letâs take another look at the loop.for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) { if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0) send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL); close(client); }This code has only two state variables, server and client. Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, weâd need to save the following state:struct Context { pc: u64, // Instruction address to return to fd_server: i32, // server file descriptor fd_client: i32, // client file descriptor }We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. Weâre playing it safe here - we donât need the full u64 or i32, and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need?$ codex "How much TCP connection takes?" Idle connection takes zero, while active connection consumes around 5kbHereâs what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment.14M idle connections - 0 bytesScheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GBOnly half of our RAM budget, yay! I donât often exceed my own expectations. Letâs validate it:int main(void) { // Run 14M of idle connections - just listen and do nothing // SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY! for (int i = 0; i < 14_000_000; i++) { int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); listen(server, 1) } }$ ./run_15m_idle_servers Out Of Memory $ dmesg | tail -n 1 'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid?Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. Iâm not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, itâs too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - letâs dive into networking in the kernel.Networking in the kernelRemember when I said that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:int main(void) { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; ++i) { socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); } }That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Letâs ask AI where all the memory goes:StructsizeofDescriptionstruct tcp_sock2240BTCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeepingstruct socket_alloc768BA 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and paddingstruct file184BOpen-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socketstruct dentry192BThe sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeepingTotal3384BPotato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some buffer: [u8; 3300], but it doesnât look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. Itâs Sunday and I have few tokens left, so weâll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel?What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we canât solve a task, weâre working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hmâ¦ level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW!The OSI model isâ¦ umâ¦ something I studied at university. Yeah, thatâs a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the application layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the transport layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, thatâs exactly what operating at the network and data link layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?Clear.Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.HTTPApplication Â· L7TCPTransport Â· L4IPNetwork Â· L3EthernetData link Â· L2PhysicalL1GET /PayloadPayloadPayloadâ¡ð©Src port50123Dst port80Seq1001ACK7001FlagsACKSrc IP192.0.2.10Dst IP198.51.100.20TTL64Protocol6 (TCP)Dst MAC02:00:00:00:00:feSrc MAC02:00:00:00:00:01EtherType0x0800 (IPv4)FCSCRCTCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkelsâs Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stackSeastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDBlwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IPF-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stackGo, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at allSo, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layerTAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layerDPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernelsmoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use.fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("tun") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?, Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip), ), Some("tap") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?, Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()), ), _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"), }; let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now()); iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| { addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap(); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant::now(); iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets); wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?; } }But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there.Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost.DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network(); receive_from_network_to_app_memory(); }Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. Letâs validate it:int main(void) { // Run 14M of idle connections - just listen and do nothing // SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY! for (int i = 0; i < 14_000_000; i++) { int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); listen(server, 1) } }$ ./run_15m_idle_servers Out Of Memory $ dmesg | tail -n 1 'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid?Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. Iâm not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, itâs too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - letâs dive into networking in the kernel.Networking in the kernelRemember when I mentioned that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:int main(void) { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; ++i) { socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); } }That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was massive and cheap, sigh. Letâs ask AI where all the memory goes:StructsizeofDescriptionstruct tcp_sock2240BTCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeepingstruct socket_alloc768BA 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and paddingstruct file184BOpen-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socketstruct dentry192BThe sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeepingTotal3384BPotato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some buffer: [u8; 3300], but it doesnât look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. Itâs Sunday and I have few tokens left, so weâll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel?What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we canât solve a task, weâre working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hmâ¦ level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW!The OSI model isâ¦ umâ¦ something I studied at university. Yeah, thatâs a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the application layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the transport layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, thatâs exactly what operating at the network and data link layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?Clear.Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.HTTPApplication Â· L7TCPTransport Â· L4IPNetwork Â· L3EthernetData link Â· L2PhysicalL1GET /PayloadPayloadPayloadâ¡ð©Src port50123Dst port80Seq1001ACK7001FlagsACKSrc IP192.0.2.10Dst IP198.51.100.20TTL64Protocol6 (TCP)Dst MAC02:00:00:00:00:feSrc MAC02:00:00:00:00:01EtherType0x0800 (IPv4)FCSCRCTCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkelsâs Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stackSeastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDBlwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IPF-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stackGo, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at allSo, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layerTAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layerDPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernelsmoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use.fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("tun") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?, Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip), ), Some("tap") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?, Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()), ), _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"), }; let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now()); iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| { addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap(); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant::now(); iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets); wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?; } }But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there.Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost.DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network(); receive_from_network_to_app_memory(); }Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.Referenceshttps://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers sourcehttps://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDKhttps://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation sitehttps://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview.

Sources indicate that what is a syscall? A function that is executed by the OS kernel. Whatever fancy language or library you use for HTTP, it all comes down to those syscalls (well, yes, but actually no). Letâs use C to make it all explicit. We start listening, then read from the socket in a loop and always reply with OK.int main(void) { // We use port 0 which makes OS return any available port int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); if (listen(server, 128) < 0) return 1; const char reply[] = "HTTP/1.0 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nOK"; for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) { if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0) send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL); close(client); } }It couldnât be simpler: listen on a socket, accept a connection, read the data, send a reply, close the client connection, and repeat. It gives us around 65k RPS. Now that weâve learned everything, letâs finish the article and call it a day:$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server &; done ... ... 28232 program exited with error 1Hm, why did listen fail? Ah, weâve run out of ports! Weâre using port=0, so the kernel picks an available port from ip_local_port_range.$ sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768 60999Why are so many ports skipped? Historically, port 0 was created for outbound connections. When you call connect('example.com', 80), Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from ip_local_port_range to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small.Port 0 is special. You cannot listen on it (actually, you can - https://acid.vegas/blog/the-port-that-does-not-exist/).Ports 1-1024 require root.Ports 1024-32768 are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You donât want to call connect('example.com') and end up allocating port 3306 to receive incoming data. mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox would make for a confusing UX.Ports 60999 - 65535 are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading.Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using 1-65535, but thatâs still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware. Letâs simply connect 15M/32k=450 upcoming network cards to the server.The 65k limit comes from the TCP standard. A port is a u16, so even if we hack the kernel with find '*.c' -exec sed -i 's/u16/u32/' \; to support bigger port numbers, normal clients still wouldnât be able to connect. Each listening server is identified by a (protocol, IP, port) tuple. That explains how we can use the same port for UDP and TCP. It also means we can use a bunch of different IPs for our web servers. If we connect 450 network cards to the server, weâll get 450 unique IP addresses and be able to listen on 15 million unique addresses!UPD. Iâve heard from readers that the network card is the ONLY hardware component that didnât get 100 times more expensive in the last year. Canât we avoid ruining that too and solve this in software?Letâs use a beautiful technology called AnyIP, which lets us listen on a whole subnet. Many VPS and dedicated server providers routinely give you a whole TCPv6 subnet. We can simply run sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo to get 18 quintillion addresses (plus or minus one) to listen on. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. Weâll change our server to pick the nth IP from our range:// Read IP index from CLI, shift base IP by it int i = read_cli_param(argv[1]); const uint32_t base_ip = 0x0a400001; // ex. 10.64.0.1 addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(first_ip + i); // shift, ex. 10.64.0.2And now we can finally finish the article.$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server $i &; done ... ... Out of memoryHm, one server consumes 1.5MB of RAM, so running that many would takeâ¦ 20TB of RAM, which is a few bytes more than our 10GB budget.RuntimeBy pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In Userland Linux scheduler in Rust, I revealed how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task.TLDR: Weâre using LFI for sandboxing. It gives us memory isolation and replaces all syscalls with calls to our host handler, which lets us implement I/O however we like. To schedule multiple guests, we load them all into our main processâs memory and make the CPU constantly switch between guests - we become our own micro OS.Since we need to save every byte and CPU cycle we can, weâre doomed to build another specialised runtime. Letâs get started. How much is 10GB divided by 15M, exactly?Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. Whatâs the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Each listening server is identified by a (protocol, IP, port) tuple. That explains how we can use the same port for UDP and TCP. It also means we can use a bunch of different IPs for our web servers. If we connect 450 network cards to the server, weâll get 450 unique IP addresses and be able to listen on 15 million unique addresses!UPD. Iâve heard from readers that the network card is the ONLY hardware component that didnât get 100 times more expensive in the last year. Canât we avoid ruining that too and solve this in software?Letâs use a beautiful technology called AnyIP, which lets us listen on a whole subnet. Many VPS and dedicated server providers routinely give you a whole TCPv6 subnet. We can simply run sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo to get 18 quintillion addresses (plus or minus one) to listen on. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. Weâll change our server to pick the nth IP from our range:// Read IP index from CLI, shift base IP by it int i = read_cli_param(argv[1]); const uint32_t base_ip = 0x0a400001; // ex. 10.64.0.1 addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(first_ip + i); // shift, ex. 10.64.0.2And now we can finally finish the article.$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server $i &; done ... ... Out of memoryHm, one server consumes 1.5MB of RAM, so running that many would takeâ¦ 20TB of RAM, which is a few bytes more than our 10GB budget.RuntimeBy pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In Userland Linux scheduler in Rust, I indicated how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task.TLDR: Weâre using LFI for sandboxing. It gives us memory isolation and replaces all syscalls with calls to our host handler, which lets us implement I/O however we like. To schedule multiple guests, we load them all into our main processâs memory and make the CPU constantly switch between guests - we become our own micro OS.Since we need to save every byte and CPU cycle we can, weâre doomed to build another specialised runtime. Letâs get started. How much is 10GB divided by 15M, exactly?Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. Whatâs the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Letâs take another look at the loop.for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) { if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0) send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL); close(client); }This code has only two state variables, server and client. Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, weâd need to save the following state:struct Context { pc: u64, // Instruction address to return to fd_server: i32, // server file descriptor fd_client: i32, // client file descriptor }We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. Weâre playing it safe here - we donât need the full u64 or i32, and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need?$ codex "How much TCP connection takes?" Idle connection takes zero, while active connection consumes around 5kbHereâs what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment.14M idle connections - 0 bytesScheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GBOnly half of our RAM budget, yay! I donât often exceed my own expectations. Letâs validate it:int main(void) { // Run 14M of idle connections - just listen and do nothing // SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY! for (int i = 0; i < 14_000_000; i++) { int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); listen(server, 1) } }$ ./run_15m_idle_servers Out Of Memory $ dmesg | tail -n 1 'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid?Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. Iâm not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, itâs too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - letâs dive into networking in the kernel.Networking in the kernelRemember when I stated that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:int main(void) { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; ++i) { socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); } }That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Letâs ask AI where all the memory goes:StructsizeofDescriptionstruct tcp_sock2240BTCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeepingstruct socket_alloc768BA 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and paddingstruct file184BOpen-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socketstruct dentry192BThe sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeepingTotal3384BPotato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some buffer: [u8; 3300], but it doesnât look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. Itâs Sunday and I have few tokens left, so weâll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel?What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we canât solve a task, weâre working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hmâ¦ level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW!The OSI model isâ¦ umâ¦ something I studied at university. Yeah, thatâs a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the application layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the transport layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, thatâs exactly what operating at the network and data link layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?Clear.Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.HTTPApplication Â· L7TCPTransport Â· L4IPNetwork Â· L3EthernetData link Â· L2PhysicalL1GET /PayloadPayloadPayloadâ¡ð©Src port50123Dst port80Seq1001ACK7001FlagsACKSrc IP192.0.2.10Dst IP198.51.100.20TTL64Protocol6 (TCP)Dst MAC02:00:00:00:00:feSrc MAC02:00:00:00:00:01EtherType0x0800 (IPv4)FCSCRCTCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkelsâs Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stackSeastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDBlwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IPF-Stack uses FreeBSDâs TCP/IP stackGo, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but theyâre nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So weâll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for >bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at allSo, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and canât do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layerTAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layerDPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernelsmoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and theyâre easy to use.fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> { let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() { Some("tun") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?, Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip), ), Some("tap") => ( TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?, Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()), ), _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"), }; let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now()); iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| { addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap(); }); let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new()); // Main network loop loop { let now = Instant::now(); iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets); wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?; } }But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: itâs common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and youâre done; when you want to read what youâve received - itâs already there.Thereâs another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but thereâs a cost.DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:loop { send_from_app_memory_to_network(); receive_from_network_to_app_memory(); }Thereâs another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers canât work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interfaceâ¦ it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, youâll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.Actually, thereâs a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.Now the final flow is:The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memoryThe runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by oneGuest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adaptersAll 15M guests start listening, each on its own addressThe scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the nextAnd now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.Referenceshttps://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers sourcehttps://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDKhttps://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation sitehttps://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview.

Hm, why did listen fail? Ah, weâve run out of ports! Weâre using port=0, so the kernel picks an available port from ip_local_port_range.$ sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768 60999Why are so many ports skipped? Historically, port 0 was created for outbound connections. When you call connect('example.com', 80), Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from ip_local_port_range to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small.Port 0 is special. You cannot listen on it (actually, you can - https://acid.vegas/blog/the-port-that-does-not-exist/).Ports 1-1024 require root.Ports 1024-32768 are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You donât want to call connect('example.com') and end up allocating port 3306 to receive incoming data. mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox would make for a confusing UX.Ports 60999 - 65535 are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading.Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using 1-65535, but thatâs still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware.
