As mitigations, customers were urged to set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release and restart the PHP worker for the setting to be applied.

The development comes nearly a month after PHP released fixes for two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively tracked as PHP2Shell that enable unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) via specially crafted HTTP requests.

The shortcomings have since come under limited active exploitation, targeting publicly-accessible Palo Alto Networks management interfaces and Check Point Security Gateways to launch attacks against Active Directory and deliver backdoors.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added four vulnerabilities impacting Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM), BerriAI LiteLLM, Apache Axis, and Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -.

"An attacker could exploit this via crafted HTTP requests that access an unintended controller route from a public survey context and supply a crafted file-path or stream parameter during data import processing," CISA remarked about CVE-2026-90817. "Exploitation requires knowledge of a valid public survey hash.".

The addition of CVE-2026-90436 to the KEV catalog follows reports that the flaw is exploited in conjunction with the 4EverAble2Shell vulnerabilities affecting N-able N-central to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers.

Rapid7, in its own analysis of the flaw, mentioned it detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center in a customer environment by taking advantage of the fact that the corporate workspace platform uses the Axis library as part of its XML-RPC and SOAP APIs.

"To be vulnerable, the Confluence instance must have the 'Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)' enabled," Atlassian mentioned. "Please note that this setting was turned off by default for upcoming installations starting in Confluence 3.0. This feature was fully removed in Confluence 10.0.".

In the activity documented by Rapid7, threat actors are stated to have weaponized the flaw to run shell commands and scripts fetched from temporary Pinggy and Cloudflare Tunnel domains, followed by enumerating the compromised environment. The incident was flagged on November 13, 2026.

"Just over three minutes after the first observed execution, the attackers were authenticating to MySQL with Confluence's own database credentials, querying page bodies, application links, and attachments with names associated with credentials, tokens, VPN configurations, and private keys," Rapid7 said.

"The attacker's scripts, likely AI-generated, then targeted files in Confluence's default location for uploaded page attachments (/var/atlassian/application-data/confluence/attachments/v4/), parsed Office documents, searched for credentials, and hunted for payment card numbers, using Luhn checks to filter out false positives.".

In addition, the attackers have been found to map various internal services, use a Confluence application credential to query the internal Atlassian Crowd API for users and group memberships, and attempt to carry out a Kerberos-based credential harvesting technique called AS-REP Roasting.

Although these efforts were unsuccessful, the threat actor managed to acquire a service account credential and queried a production cloud data warehouse. About 12 hours after the first exploit request, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 as an integration service account using legacy authentication from "192.238.253[.]176.".

It has been revealed that CVE-2026-90436, which affects Axis 1.x versions, remains unpatched as Axis 1 has reached end-of-life (EoL) status. It's recommended to migrate to a different SOAP engine, such as Apache Axis 2/Java. Alternatively, users can use a build of Axis with the patch from a July 12, 2026, commit applied.

As for CVE-2026-90817, Safe Security said in a report published late last month that it observed an unknown threat abusing the flaw to "stage a transient web shell, followed by an in-memory loader that retrieved XMRig disguised as image files, masqueraded the miner as syslog-ng, and established persistence through cron and an added SSH key.".

The exploitation of CVE-2026-40217 stems from a Google Threat Intelligence Group report this week in which threat actors have leveraged the vulnerability to elevate limited-access inference keys into full administrative credentials and establish persistence as part of LLMjacking attacks aimed at financial services, retail, transportation, and technology organizations in North America, South America, and the Asia Pacific region.

Rounding off the list is CVE-2024-10441, which Synology disclosed earlier this month as being exploited in ransomware attacks targeting Network Attached Storage (NAS) devices. The attacks have been found to result in the deployment of C3RB3R ransomware.

In light of active exploitation, federal agencies have been recommended to apply fixes or necessary mitigations for DSM, REDCap, and Axis flaws by November 21, 2026, and for the LiteLLM flaw by December 2, 2026.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Low-privilege database accounts that cannot read a single application table can still be used to run code on the database server itself, a researcher has shown, by reaching memory-corruption bugs in the engine code behind ordinary SQL.
  • The exploits, published yesterday, are the researcher's proofs of concept against PostgreSQL, MySQL and ClickHouse, plus a separate Oracle chain that needs no login.
  • Recent findings suggest that the work is by Zheng Yu, a researcher at Depthfirst.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Low-privilege database accounts that cannot read a single application table can still be used to run code on the database server itself, a researcher has shown, by reaching memory-corruption bugs in the engine code behind ordinary SQL.

The exploits, published yesterday, are the researcher's proofs of concept against PostgreSQL, MySQL and ClickHouse, plus a separate Oracle chain that needs no login. None has been seen in a real attack.

Recent findings suggest that the work is by Zheng Yu, a researcher at Depthfirst. A database account's SQL permissions control which tables and schemas it can access, the researcher argues, not the memory-unsafe C and C++ code the engine runs to read, proposal, and execute a query.

Industry observers note that common grants give an account enough room to reach that code. PostgreSQL's default TEMPORARY privilege, or the right to create temporary tables in MySQL and ClickHouse, allows an account to create objects or send input that triggers a memory bug.

Four of the flaws now have vendor CVEs and fixes, but the full attack chains were not reproduced independently, and the research reports no sign that any of them has been used in an attack.

In PostgreSQL, the flaw CVE-2026-116331 allows an account that can create database objects to run code as the operating system user that runs the database.

It was fixed last week in a security advisory, and the CVE record credits the researcher for the report. The researcher's technical analysis indicates a plain login role building the objects it needs in its own temporary schema, without touching application data, then turning a type-confusion bug into control of the server.

MySQL has a similar flaw in its query optimizer, CVE-2026-101786, in Server and Cluster versions 26.7.0 to 26.7.1. Oracle's MySQL October advisory rates it as needing high privileges.

The researcher reached code execution on the 26.7.0 image with an account that could only create temporary tables and could not read existing ones, a narrower kind of access than that rating suggests.

According to recent reports, oracle Database is the one case where an attacker needs no account at all, the researcher states. A bug in Oracle Text and a flaw in the GraphQL interface of Oracle REST Data Services, chained against an exposed web endpoint, reach the engine code and run commands before any login.

Sources indicate that oracle patched the Oracle Text bug, CVE-2026-114819, rated 9.9, earlier this week in its November revision, and the GraphQL flaw, CVE-2026-91609, in the October update. On their own, the manufacturer rates neither as exploitable without a login.

Recent findings suggest that clickHouse is the fourth target. The researcher reports an integer-overflow write in how it reads a binary row format, reached by a user who sets a single option, format_binary_max_string_size, to zero, and reproduced a shell on version 26.7.5.10.

This one has no CVE and no confirmed fixed version, so operators should check with the vendor for the fix.

Beyond installing the updates, the other move is to review what accounts can do, not only what they can read, and to take away the TEMPORARY privilege and broad temporary-table rights from accounts that do not need them. That step does not close the Oracle path, which starts without any account.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there was an error while loading. Please reload this page.

In a recent development, there was an error while loading. Please reload this page.

In StubGenerator::generate_base64_decodeBlock() (x86_64 AVX-512 VBMI path), L_finalBit handles 1-63 leftover bytes with a masked vector sequence that computes output_size = (len/4)*3. Valid inputs always have a length multiple of 4, so this bug triggers only on invalid inputs: with length < 4 (e.g. "A".repeat(64)+"=" leaves 1 byte after L_process64Loop), output_size starts at 0 and the padding path decrements it below zero, producing a wrong output_mask. The stub stores past the logical output length before returning to Java, corrupting the heap.

The suggested fix is to early-return to Java if length < 4.

  • It has been revealed that last week, Microsoft shipped ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 as part of the wider .NET 11 release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News .NET 11 : ASP.NET Core: Union Type Support, OpenAPI 3.2 by Default and Blazor AI Components.

Nov 19, 2026 3 min read.

It has been revealed that last week, Microsoft shipped ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 as part of the wider .NET 11 release. The update spans Minimal APIs, OpenAPI, SignalR, Blazor, authentication, and the Kestrel server. As stated in the announcement, .NET 11 is a Standard Term Support release with two years of support.

Recent findings suggest that on the API side, developers can now use C# 15 union types in JSON request and response bodies across Minimal APIs and MVC. The release notes limit the feature to JSON bodies, so route, query, header, and form values cannot bind to a union.

Minimal API validation also runs asynchronous validators, which keeps threads free while a rule waits on a database lookup or a remote call. The framework can now localize validation messages and display names itself, and endpoints can skip the remaining middleware pipeline through a new [ShortCircuit] attribute.

Developers who generate OpenAPI documents now get version 3.2 unless they select an earlier one for tooling that has not caught up. As described in the release notes, the framework depends on Microsoft.OpenApi 3.3.1 for this, and the notes label that revision a breaking change.

With 3.2, endpoints that stream server-sent events are documented with a schema for each event's payload, and the generator emits an anyOf schema for unions. Generated documents can also describe endpoints that use the HTTP QUERY method, and APIs that carry the [Obsolete] attribute show up as deprecated.

SignalR adds authentication refresh, so a long-lived connection no longer has to close when its access token expires. As reported, server developers enable it per hub, while the .NET client refreshes automatically by default and the TypeScript client can do the same. Blazor passes the refreshed identity on to Interactive Server components while the circuit stays connected.

According to recent reports, blazor receives the longest list of changes, and many of them target static server-side rendering. With the latest CacheView component, developers can cache the rendered markup of a component subtree, and the child components do not run when a cached copy is served. Blazor now ships client-side validation for static SSR forms, enabled by default.

According to recent reports, developers can also carry data between requests with TempData or session values. According to the release notes, the Blazor Web App template drops its app.UseAntiforgery() call, because a middleware for CSRF protection is now added by default.

For Interactive Server apps, an opt-in package pauses the circuit of a hidden browser tab after a delay, two minutes by default, to free server memory. Lists built with Virtualize may now mix items of different heights, and Microsoft raised the default OverscanCount from 3 to 15. Page and sort state in QuickGrid now lives in the URL query string, with sortable headers and pager controls rendered as links instead of buttons.

The release notes flag this as a CSS breaking change, because custom styles written for the buttons also have to target the links. The release also includes Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.AI, a set of components for chat and agent interfaces. According to the announcement, Microsoft treats that package as experimental and will keep it in prerelease throughout .NET 11.

Recent findings suggest that on the security and server side, an experimental package adds Device Bound Session Credentials, a protocol that ties session refresh to a private key held by the browser. Response compression and request decompression gain Zstandard support, which is on by default.

Sources indicate that kestrel's HTTP/1.1 parser no longer throws exceptions on malformed requests, a change that is reported to raise throughput by up to 20 to 40 percent under heavy invalid traffic. The shared framework libraries of ASP.NET Core are now compiled with runtime-async, described in the release notes as an internal change with no public API impact.

Sources indicate that two older APIs are on the way out. The Microsoft.AspNetCore.Grpc.Swagger package is now deprecated, and Kestrel's TlsClientHelloBytesCallback option is obsolete in favor of the new UseTlsClientHelloListener extension.

Other changes in this release are native OpenTelemetry tracing attributes, client-side cancellation of SignalR hub invocations, scrolling to a specific item in Virtualize and QuickGrid, passkey display names inferred from the authenticator, and TimeProvider support in ASP.NET Core Identity.

For interested readers and developers, the full release notes are available in the What's fresh in ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 article on Microsoft Learn.

  • "We are aware of PoCs that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution," the maintainers said.
  • The project released fixed versions yesterday: Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ruby contains seven memory-safety flaws in its regular expression engine and its string case-conversion code. For five of them, its maintainers say, proof-of-concept exploits, or PoCs, have shown that crafted input can run code on the machine.

"We are aware of PoCs that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution," the maintainers said.

The project released fixed versions yesterday: Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14. Whether an application is at risk depends on whether an attacker can get crafted patterns or strings into the affected code, and the advisories report no attacks so far.

Sources indicate that the other two flaws are weaker. The maintainers say one has proof-of-concept code that corrupts memory under an attacker's control but has not been shown to run code, and the other can only read memory it should not or crash the program.

The project set the seven out in a security announcement and a separate advisory for each. The advisories rate three flaws critical, three high, and one moderate, and say which carry the remote-code-execution PoCs. In order of severity:.

The project credits Stephan Lipp of Ada Logics and Anthropic with four of the findings, and baba__yaga, aphantom, Hiroya Fujinami and Hiroshi SHIBATA with the other three.

Recent findings suggest that the flaws are in Ruby's own code, so every application on an affected version carries them. Whether an attacker can reach one depends on how the application handles external input.

The regex flaws need an application that builds a regular expression from input an attacker controls and then compiles or runs it. Matching untrusted text against a pattern the developers wrote themselves does not pose the same risk, except in one case below.

The two case-conversion flaws do not involve regular expressions at all. They fire when the application changes the case of a crafted string, so code that runs case conversion over imported or outside text is worth checking.

In a recent development, the one case is the moderate read flaw, which fires when the application matches a crafted subject string against a fixed pattern that uses a case-insensitive backreference. The announcement and advisories do not include the proof-of-concept code.

The fixes are in Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14. The affected ranges are:.

Those older versions will not get a fix, and the project recommends moving to a supported line. With 3.3.14, the maintainers renamed the Ruby 3.3 phase from security maintenance to legacy maintenance, and support still ends at the end of March 2027.

According to recent reports, because the fixes ship inside Ruby, updating an application's gems or framework does not replace a vulnerable interpreter. The version that matters is the Ruby running on application servers, background workers, and container images, which must be updated and then restarted or rebuilt.

The seven do not have CVE numbers yet. The project states it has requested them, and until they are assigned, the GitHub advisory IDs are the only way to track flaws in scanners and software inventories.

According to recent reports, it is the second time in a month that the project has patched its regular expression engine. In the October fixes, released on October 23, it shipped Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12, and 3.3.13 to patch compilation bugs GitLab found, which sat behind four critical GitLab flaws.

One of those GitLab flaws drew an attempted attack on Alpine Linux's own GitLab server. CISA later added it to the KEV catalog, its list of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, as actively exploited.

Those are different bugs from this week's seven, and the latest advisories do not say that GitLab or any other named product can be attacked through them. What the October case showed is that a regular expression built from user input can become a real way onto a server, not just a theoretical one.

  • Nov 19, 2026 4 min read.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Use AI to Multiply Your Team as a Staff Engineer.

Nov 19, 2026 4 min read.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Jordan Cutler, Senior Staff Engineer and Web Platform Tech Lead at Pinterest, presented how the role of a staff engineer changes when every engineer has access to the same AI tools. The session argued that most "AI for engineers" content focuses on individual productivity, while the real question for staff engineers is where their leverage comes from now. According to Cutler, AI did not change what a staff engineer is for, but it changed where the leverage is.

Recent findings suggest that the talk opened with a reflection on Cutler's previous conference talk, where he showed how AI could turn a four-hour task into four minutes. At that point he was shipping roughly as much as his whole team, which he described as multiplying himself rather than his team. That framed the central question of the session: what does a 10x engineer look like when everyone has AI?

To illustrate why this matters, Cutler shared internal Pinterest data on merged pull requests per engineer per week between Q1 2025 and Q3 2026. The top 10% of engineers went from 6.7 to 11.3 merged PRs per week, a 68% increase, while the bottom half went from 1.0 to 1.15, an increase of 14%. Everyone has AI, but not everyone uses it the same way, and the gap keeps growing. The presentation organized the response to that gap into three moves: multiply yourself, multiply your team, and multiply the system.

The first move, multiply yourself, is about going first. Cutler explained that he tries new tools before his team does, and that part of that work is hitting dead ends so others don't have to. He mentioned examples such as an agent harness that could not be steered mid-task and a remote agent runner that required too many follow-ups. Sharing those findings early means the team does not lose a week on the same experiments. Running many agents also revealed a new problem: he kept giving the same corrections in every session, such as avoiding em-dashes, adding a diagram to the PR description, and keeping pull requests small.

According to recent reports, the second move, multiply your team, started from a limitation: the folder made him faster, but only he had it. With upcoming people joining the team and a new area to ramp up on, Cutler found himself repeating the same comments in code review, such as asking why a value is null instead of fixing the cause, testing like a user would, and keeping PRs small. The talk emphasized that the value of encoding that judgment grows with every teammate who adopts it, compared to the flat curve of a single engineer working alone.

Recent findings suggest that the third move, multiply the system, is about moving up a level. Cutler used the history of container shipping as an analogy: ports got better at loading cargo by hand, but the standard box changed the economics entirely, from $5.86 a ton to 16 cents a ton. At Pinterest, migrations were the cargo, one kind of change spread across hundreds of files and dozens of teams. Instead of running each migration by hand, the team built a system where a staff engineer points to a plan and an example, an engineer puts it on a schedule, and an agent running in a sandbox splits the work into PRs team by team. A class component migration ran three to five times faster than by hand, in the background while teams worked on other things.

The talk also covered what went wrong. One scheduled job looped and opened 16 PRs in two minutes, increasing CI wait times from under 30 seconds to 14 minutes. The lesson was not to wait for the perfect guardrail, but to ship a small one. Cutler encouraged attendees to find their own "any" problem: a first responder for any incident, a draft fix for any bug ticket, or an agent that triages any flaky test. Today, 40 engineers have scheduler jobs of their own.

The results were significant. Using the same AI tools as other web teams, Cutler's team now ships about four times as much per engineer, without counting his own PRs.

Industry observers note that the presentation concluded with practical steps: write down what you repeat, put it where people already work, and build for every case instead of one. Some parts of the job cannot be written down, like an honest conversation with a teammate who is struggling, and those remain the staff engineer's responsibility. As Cutler put it, a 10x engineer isn't ten times faster, they are the reason ten other people are. As AI agents become part of everyday development workflows, the role of senior engineers may increasingly shift from personal output toward encoding judgment into the tools, defaults, and systems that entire organizations use.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A few months ago, I wrote about how I started giving away zines to my friends, my family, and people at work.

It has been revealed that if you've never made one, the fold is simple. Take a single A4 sheet of paper, fold it in half three times, open it back up, and cut along the center crease with scissors. Fold the sheet into a cross and close it, and you have an 8-page booklet with no staples or glue.

I fill mine with whatever I feel like printing: photos, poems, or notes.

The part I never liked was laying out the flat sheet on the computer before printing. Because the A4 paper folds back on itself, the pages sit in a strange order and the top row has to be upside down:.

I got tired of rotating pictures and double-checking columns in Photoshop every time I wanted to print a latest zine, so I built fanzines.app.

In a recent development, in the browser, you lay out each page right-side up with photos and text. When you export, the app places all 8 panels onto the A4 grid with the top row rotated 180 degrees and generates a 300 DPI PDF. Everything stays local in the browser; no photos are uploaded to a server.

Over the last few days, I rebuilt the editor around the things that kept getting in my way when I sat down to make a zine.

Sources indicate that in the first version, the sidebar listed the 8 pages in a plain two-column grid. It paired the Front Cover with Page 1, Page 2 with Page 3, Page 4 with Page 5, and Page 6 with the Back Cover.

Recent findings suggest that it looked tidy on screen, but it didn't match the physical booklet. When you hold a folded zine, the front cover sits alone on the right. Open it and Page 1 faces Page 2 across the fold, then 3 faces 4, 5 faces 6, and the back cover ends up alone on the left.

The sidebar now groups the page thumbnails into those real spreads, in reading order.

Sources indicate that I also added a Spread view on the canvas. While you're editing Page 1, Page 2 sits beside it at lower opacity so you can check how the two facing pages sit together before printing. Clicking the dimmed page switches straight to editing it.

When I make a photo zine, I usually start with a folder of 8 photos already picked out. Now you can drag the whole batch onto the editor window, and the sidebar highlights which pages will take each photo in reading order before you drop them.

I changed the side panel too. Early on, clicking a photo opened four coordinate inputs (X, Y, Width, Height). I rarely needed to type coordinates; mostly I wanted a photo to fill the page, fit inside the margins, or sit centered. Fill, Fit, and Center now sit at the top of the inspector and in a small toolbar above the selection.

The exact fields are still in a collapsible section at the bottom, now in millimeters (for the 74.25 × 105 mm folded panel) and points for text.

Recent findings suggest that before downloading the PDF, a Review step indicates the full unfolded A4 sheet with toggles for cut/fold lines and a 5 mm safe margin. Most home printers clip a few millimeters around the edge of an A4 sheet, so the safe margin scales the layout to about 95% to keep the covers intact.

Industry observers note that A couple of other additions: the editor now works on phone screens (one page at a time with a thumbnail strip along the bottom), and the site is available in English as well as Spanish. Changing the language keeps your current pages.

You can create your own zine in English or Spanish at fanzines.app.

#544. Breaking: 0.58.0 and v0.58.0 Are the Same Version. Our Code Disagreed.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1064 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

Breaking: 0.58.0 and v0.58.0 Are the Same Version. Our Code Disagreed.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Nov 18 I asked our own API a simple question: what changed in golang.org/x/net since 0.58.0?
  • We just had them stored as v0.58.0, with a v, because that's how the Go module proxy writes them.
  • That one answer turned into a day of finding every place in our code that compared versions as plain text.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov 18 I asked our own API a simple question: what changed in golang.org/x/net since 0.58.0?

It told me the package wasn't in the catalog.

It was. We had every release of it. We just had them stored as v0.58.0, with a v, because that's how the Go module proxy writes them. I had typed it without the v, the way plenty of people type it in issues, in chat, and apparently in my own head.

That one answer turned into a day of finding every place in our code that compared versions as plain text. There were a lot of them.

Since tracks what code depends on (packages, AI models, APIs, runtimes) and tells people and their coding agents what changed. So "what changed since version X" is the question we answer more than any other. And version X shows up in whatever spelling the asker's tools happen to use.

Here's the whole problem in a few lines. Each pair is the same version, as two real tools write it:.

Run with Node 24 in an empty folder, it prints:.

Recent findings suggest that five pairs, five false. Every one of them is the same version to the person who wrote it.

Industry observers note that the embarrassing part wasn't the bug. It was what we found when we went looking for it.

Different parts of the codebase had each run into one spelling at some point and patched for it right there. The Go v had been added back by hand in six different files. A short 13.0 was written out to 13.0.0 in one place. Everywhere else, a version that wasn't spelled exactly like the stored one just didn't match.

So the answer you got depended on which door your version came in through:.

It has been revealed that that last one deserves a footnote. Java called itself 1.2, 1.3, all the way to 1.8, and then Java 9 dropped the "1." for good. So every tool that's been around long enough still writes Java 8 as 1.8, and every list of release lines calls it 8. Both are right. They just never meet.

Nothing crashed. That's what made it bad. A version that didn't match didn't throw an error, it quietly got a smaller answer, and a smaller answer looks exactly like a correct one.

The worst one was in security advisories for Go.

Sources indicate that of the 12,714 Go advisories we had stored, 10,337 carried the advisory database's spelling of a version, like 0.62.0, next to the Go proxy's v0.62.0. Our answers and our fix emails printed the advisory's spelling.

Go's tools want the v. Paste go get golang.org/x/net@0.62.0 and Go refuses it. So for about 81% of Go advisories, the "upgrade to" version we demonstrated was one you couldn't paste.

At that point it stops being an edge case. It's the main case, wearing an edge case costume.

The obvious fix was a seventh patch: add the v back in one more place, ship it, go to lunch.

Sources indicate that I'd already seen where that road goes. It goes to six files, each with its own little opinion about what a version looks like, each one right about the one spelling it had met and wrong about the rest.

So we did it once instead. Each registry gets one rule for what "the same version" means, written the way that registry's own tools read a version:.

Recent findings suggest that then every place that takes a version from the outside world (a question, a manifest, a lockfile, an advisory) asks that one rule before it compares anything. The six local patches got deleted, which was the most satisfying diff of the week.

The part I'm actually proudest of is what we refused to merge.

It has been revealed that some places really do treat two spellings as two different things. A Docker tag or a GitHub Actions ref is the same only when it's written the same: a tag named v4 and one named 4 can point at completely different things. So there, text comparison stays. A "smart" normalizer that stripped every v everywhere would have been a brand newly introduced bug with a nice commit message.

Then the same disease showed up somewhere I didn't expect: type signatures.

We read the code of package releases, so we can tell you when a function you call changed shape. That diff compared signatures as text. So in Python, List[str] and list[str] counted as a breaking change. So did Optional[bytes] and bytes | None. In TypeScript, Array and string[]. In Go, interface{} and any.

We measured it on production data, read only. Of the stored code-only signature changes, these were nothing but respellings:.

One in six PyPI "signature changes" was Python learning to write list in lowercase.

According to recent reports, same fix, same caution. Compare what the language itself indicates is one type, and nothing more. TypeScript's ?: T and ?: T | undefined stay different, because TypeScript treats them differently. A parameter's name stays part of it wherever callers can pass it by name.

And one more, because it made me laugh: Guava ships most releases twice, as -android and -jre. We were reading the difference between the two flavors of the same release as changes. That was 88 of Guava's 100 newest steps. A version now stays on its own flavor's line.

Since Nov 18 this is live. You can ask the way your tools write it and get the same answer as the registry's own spelling:.

I checked this morning (Nov 19). Asking what changed in golang.org/x/net since 0.58.0 now answers from v0.58.0: five releases behind the latest, v0.63.0. And go1.20 comes back as Go 1.20, end of life Feb 6, 2024.

Industry observers note that when you catch yourself writing the same small fix in a second place, the spelling isn't the bug. The bug is that nobody owns the question "are these two the same?" Give that question one owner, send every input through it, and be exactly as careful about what it must never merge as about what it should.

What's the strangest version string a tool has ever insisted on in your codebase?

#541. Decide what meeting-room AI must run on the device

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1074 w)

Decide what meeting-room AI must run on the device

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1074 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that tormod Ree, chief product and engineering officer at Neat, describes meeting rooms with 11 or more cameras and dozens of microphones.
  • Ree ranks the case for edge AI as time sensitivity first, privacy second, and cost third.
  • So we do a combination of edge and cloud.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that tormod Ree, chief product and engineering officer at Neat, describes meeting rooms with 11 or more cameras and dozens of microphones. The system has to tell who is present, who is talking, and who is looking at whom, then choose what a remote participant sees and hears. That choice sits on the live media path. Where you run it is the design decision.

Ree ranks the case for edge AI as time sensitivity first, privacy second, and cost third. He places cost behind the other two. Processing on the path of seeing and hearing people has to run on the device. That covers detecting people, detecting who is speaking, picking a camera, and mixing microphones. Neat uses both edge and cloud. The split follows the job.

Yes. So we do a combination of edge and cloud. We sort of do it where it makes sense, but typically sort of arguments for doing it at the edge in probably an order of importance is kind of time sensitivity, privacy and cost.

Tormod Ree, chief product and engineering officer at Neat.

Privacy is a training constraint as well as a runtime one. The devices sit in rooms where the conversations are private. Neat cannot simply collect customer meetings as training data. Ree describes internally sourced material and relevant public datasets, with relatively little synthetic data. He ties that to local processing: what happens locally stays locally and is processed locally.

Slower work belongs in another bucket. Fleet management can wait. In one mode, audio summaries run in the cloud because they are less time sensitive. Neat processes that audio during the meeting or as the meeting closes. Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, and Zoom remain cloud meeting services. That cloud path is the call. The framing that makes the room watchable stays on the hardware in the room.

Latency for a language model separates time-to-first-token from the time until the model finishes. A framing decision has a different output: which video stream, which crop, which microphone mix. If it lands late, the remote person is looking at the wrong face or hearing the wrong mic. The latency glossary notes that a 100-millisecond interaction and a ten-second one are different products even at identical quality. Ree does not state a millisecond cap for the camera cut. I would set the budget from the failure you can see. If the step must finish while that person is still in frame and still talking, run it on the device next to the sensors. If the user needs the result only after the meeting, cloud is allowed.

Industry observers note that keep the coordinating device light. Ree describes a captain, usually at the front of the room, with microphones, cameras, speakers, and the screen. Other devices, including a unit at the table, each run their own audio or video inference. They send metadata along with media. The captain selects and mixes from that metadata, and can skip a second inference pass on the incoming streams. Inference and orchestration both stay at the edge. When one chip is not enough, he adds devices. A camera unit or a microphone unit still has compute, so the room picks up more of it.

Sources indicate that the rules that turn those signals into a layout are still mostly deterministic. Someone talks, or the headcount crosses a threshold, and a fixed rule picks the experience.

the decisions that you make to produce the end, the result experience, those algorithms are still to a large extent deterministic, right?

Tormod Ree, chief product and engineering officer at Neat.

He expects that director to become a trained model later. The shift has not happened. It needs probably more of this kind of data than most companies have, and a decent amount of compute. The devices are typically Android, in the class of a phone: the mobile compute available when that hardware was designed. A five-year life, which customers often expect, means living with something like a new phone from five years earlier. A Mac Mini with a lot of memory is a richer box, and a cloud GPU is another class entirely. Models he still runs locally have to stay narrow and targeted. I would keep the director as explicit rules until a trained model beats those rules on devices already in rooms.

Recent findings suggest that ree says detectors that find people, and detectors that tell who is talking, have moved a long way. The harder layer is nonverbal signal, such as someone standing or presenting, and combining cameras and microphones so the room acts as one system rather than one powerful device at the front. A speech miss and a bad crop show up in different tests. Score them apart.

In a recent development, for speech, use word error rate. Align the recognizer output with a human transcript, count insertions, deletions, and substitutions, and divide by the number of words in the reference. That glossary cites rough bands for one speech service: 5 to 10% as good quality, around 20% as acceptable though it may need more training, and 30% or more as a sign it needs customization. The bands depend on the audio and the task, so treat them as a starting point. I would read the error mix before I read the single percentage. Many deletions usually trace to a weak signal, insertions to noise or crosstalk, and substitutions to domain terms the model has not seen enough of. Word error rate scores words. It can hold steady while the camera frames the wrong person.

Sources indicate that for vision, label the events the product acts on: a person present, a person looking at someone, a person standing, a person presenting. Report misses and false alarms for each event. Room size, acoustics, and how people interact all vary, which is why the test has to be a real room. Ree claims meeting-room scenes differ from a security camera, a car, or the sets you typically find online, so the model has to be trained and tested on relevant data.

When word error rate moves and the vision rates hold, look at the microphones and the speech model. When a vision event rate moves and word error rate holds, look at that detector. Publish the two reports together.

#540. Tech Report: Everything Is a Web Application, Including Your Firewall

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1026 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thehackernews

Tech Report: Everything Is a Web Application, Including Your Firewall

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1026 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thehackernews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, one of the early targets of PHP2Shell exploitation was the firewall.
  • The vulnerabilities require no authentication, but they are not easy to exploit reliably.
  • It has been revealed that everything is a web application.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, one of the early targets of PHP2Shell exploitation was the firewall. On October 28, Palo Alto Networks confirmed that attackers were exploiting the two PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. Both flaws let anyone execute code on the web server without authentication. The disclosure itself went a little wrong. Details leaked on October 20, ahead of the coordinated release, and the PHP project shipped an emergency patch the next day.

The vulnerabilities require no authentication, but they are not easy to exploit reliably. It takes skill and additional knowledge about the target system. Where it matters a lot is appliances, which run identical, often outdated software that an attacker can study in advance. That is the bigger picture. An awful lot of web applications control critical devices in your network. Almost anything is a web application to some extent. That often goes unrecognized, and as a result those applications aren't adequately protected.

It has been revealed that everything is a web application. That is the motto of the SANS course I teach, SEC522: Application Security: Securing Web Applications, APIs, and Microservices. Web application security has traditionally been treated as a developer matter, yet anyone protecting a network must understand how web applications work to properly defend them.

In a recent development, on ordinary web servers, address space layout randomization (ASLR) is one of the features that makes exploitation harder. It shuffles where code and data sit in memory, so an exploit can't rely on fixed addresses. VulnCheck's early analysis found the bugs exploitable on ARM64 systems and on x86 systems without ASLR. Few public exploits bypassed ASLR on x86-64, and the one VulnCheck confirmed worked only against a single PHP build. VulnCheck's own exploit chained a memory leak to get code execution with ASLR enabled.

Web application security tends to focus on large, cloud-based applications. It's often the little things, the mosquitoes on the internet, that do you in. Appliances run predictable, often outdated software, and they are everywhere.

It has been revealed that HTTP is a very complex protocol with lots of options. To upload a file, a client doesn't have to send it in one piece. It can send the body in chunks without declaring its total length, and, if the server decompresses request bodies, compress it, which makes it difficult for a web server to calculate how much memory it needs to store it. Memory-safety bugs remain common as a result, in web applications and in the web servers running them. In PHP2Shell, a crafted multipart upload pushes PHP past its memory limit while it is still parsing the request, before any application code runs. The bugs are in what PHP leaves behind when it aborts the request: uninitialized request memory (CVE-2026-109618) and a pointer to freed memory (CVE-2026-109619). The request doesn't need to be large, either. Deeply nested, empty file fields make PHP allocate far more memory than the body contains, so a request well under the default 8 MB post_max_size can still exhaust the default 128 MB memory limit.

Sources indicate that defenders must understand the protocol to know what these vulnerabilities look like, for example to write signatures that detect the exploits. The same complexity limits the middle boxes we rely on. They can even interfere in ways nobody planned. Intruder found that nginx in front of PAN-OS buffered chunked request bodies, which broke public exploit chains. Web application firewalls are often not adequate, and file uploads are key functionality for a lot of web applications, so blocking them outright isn't an option.

That takes out many of the traditional defenses. What remains is knowing where your critical web applications are. Identify them, starting with the admin interfaces on your firewalls and other network equipment, and restrict access to them. Palo Alto's own guidance for PHP2Shell was to remove internet access to management interfaces and limit them to trusted internal IP addresses. If you rely on a web application firewall, configure it properly and understand how much protection it does and doesn't provide.

Industry observers note that the clearest lesson from PHP2Shell is how difficult it can be to accurately determine the risk from a vulnerability like this. Prioritization is always a big problem for defenders, particularly with today's flood of vulnerabilities, and this one was hard to read from every angle.

Industry observers note that the scores told different stories. The PHP project rated both flaws 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, and Fortinet's PSIRT listed 9.8 under CVSS v3. Palo Alto initially scored the glitch 8.7 for its own products and listed it at moderate urgency, raised it to 9.2 Critical with the highest urgency on October 27, and confirmed exploitation a week after its advisory went out. Many public proofs of concept didn't work, so a flood of attempts in your logs mentioned little about whether a given server was at risk. And PHP core developer Gina Peter Banyard warned that one early workaround, turning off session upload progress, was not enough on its own.

We are adding these lessons to SEC522: how to assess risk, how protections like ASLR reduce it, and why appliances remain softer targets.

I will be teaching SEC522: Application Security: Securing Web Applications, APIs, and Microservices at SANS Cyber Defense Initiative 2026, December 14-18 in Washington, D.C., and Live Online. The course starts with how HTTP works, including HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, and covers file upload handling, API security, and AI endpoints across 17 hands-on labs and a Defend the Flag capstone. It is built for the people who defend web applications, whether or not they wrote them.

Register for SEC522 at SANS Cyber Defense Initiative 2026.

Note: This article has been written and contributed by Dr. Johannes Ullrich, Dean of Research at SANS Technology Institute.

It has been revealed that this article starts from an operations question, « which change moved the cost, and where can I see it? », rather than from a feature tour. The topic is separate from our article on effective CPU requests, which tunes a pod’s resources. Here we turn those resources into money.

In a recent development, one limit to keep in mind: OpenCost estimates and allocates spend. It replaces neither the provider invoice nor a performance analysis.

To judge whether a number is credible, you need the recipe. The specification splits total cluster cost into two families: assets (nodes, volumes, disks, load balancers, network traffic) and overhead, such as cluster management fees.

Recent findings suggest that an asset costs either an allocation (you pay for reserved time, whatever the usage) or a usage (you pay per unit, such as bytes egressed). The documentation gives the formulas.

In a recent development, the second line matters most for decisions. Workload costs plus idle costs plus overhead equal total cost. Idle cost is the share of allocated resources that no workload claims. An oversized cluster is therefore never « free »: its spend reappears in that line.

The README claims installation goes through the official Helm chart only, on Kubernetes 1.20 or later; the standalone manifests were removed:.

Mind a nuance in the documentation. The installation page calls Prometheus a prerequisite for scraping and storage, with a PROMETHEUS_SERVER_ENDPOINT variable to point at your server. The integration page states that a Prometheus client is not needed to emit the cost metrics. The two statements can be reconciled: OpenCost reads its input data from Prometheus and can then expose its own metrics. I did not verify this on a cluster.

It has been revealed that the expected inputs come from node-exporter (for example node_cpu_seconds_total) and kube-state-metrics (for example kube_pod_container_resource_requests). If your Prometheus already scrapes kube-state-metrics, the documentation warns of possible duplicate metrics. A sharded Prometheus needs a global query endpoint such as Thanos Query or Mimir; see our article on Mimir for that storage layer.

The API listens on port 9003 of the service by default. The documentation demonstrates how to reach it locally, then three typical queries:.

Three parameters shape how you read the result:.

The resolution parameter trades accuracy against memory: 1 minute by default, finer for short-lived pods, cheaper in queries with a larger value. For a ten-minute job, avoid a coarse resolution.

This is where the topic leaves finance. OpenCost exposes its results as Prometheus metrics. A single scrape configuration puts them next to your latencies and error rates.

The documentation also offers starter queries, for example sum(node_total_hourly_cost) * 730 for the monthly cost of all nodes, or sum(kubecost_load_balancer_cost) by (namespace) for load balancers per namespace. The kubecost_ prefix on some metrics is a legacy of the original project.

Three practical uses come out of this join:.

Sources indicate that for Prometheus versus OpenTelemetry, see our comparison. What I read about OpenCost goes through Prometheus; I did not verify a native OpenTelemetry export.

The README describes an MCP server, disabled by default and enabled with --set opencost.mcp.enabled=true, listening on port 8081. It exposes get_allocation_costs, get_asset_costs, get_cloud_costs and get_efficiency (rightsizing recommendations), among others. An agent could then answer « which namespace grew most this week? ». As with any agent, scope its access before opening it: see our analysis of SRE agent promises.

Recent findings suggest that the code is Apache 2.0 and the documentation is CC BY 4.0. The cost of the cluster that hosts it, and of Prometheus, stays with you.

No. It allocates and estimates spend from prices and metrics. Always reconcile its total with the invoice.

The installation documentation describes it as a prerequisite, with a configurable endpoint. The integration page states that a Prometheus client is not needed to emit the cost metrics.

According to recent reports, openCost is worth a trial if « who costs what » comes up at every invoice review. Start with one cluster, a seven-day window and namespace aggregation, then overlay the result on your releases. Sources: the OpenCost documentation and the opencost/opencost repository.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yup is a schema validation library for JavaScript that lets you describe the shape of your data once, then validate it anywhere — in a form, in an API request, or in a test. Instead of writing nested if statements to check that an email looks like an email and a password is long enough, you write a schema that reads almost like English.

Recent findings suggest that what makes Yup different is its builder API. You chain methods to describe each field: what type it is, whether it is required, and what counts as valid. The schema then produces clear, field-specific error messages, and it can also cast and transform values before they reach your code.

A signup form schema highlights how readable it is:.

It has been revealed that yup is a great fit for forms, API validation, and anywhere untrusted input enters your app. It pairs naturally with Formik and React Hook Form, and the same schema can validate on the client and on the server.

According to recent reports, the limits are honest ones. Yup adds a dependency where a few manual checks might do, and its error messages need customizing for a polished product. Very complex conditional rules can get verbose. But for form validation, that trade is usually worth it.

Next time you build a form, try Yup for one schema first: define it, validate a bad input, and read the errors. You will know within an hour whether it earns a permanent place in your toolkit.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Under specific conditions, a critical vulnerability in Drupal core can allow an attacker without login credentials to use the built-in installer to attempt to reinstall a site.
  • That can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution, and the project rates the vulnerable configurations as uncommon.
  • The Drupal Security Team disclosed the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-132165, yesterday and rated it critical, 18 out of 25 on the project's risk scale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Under specific conditions, a critical vulnerability in Drupal core can allow an attacker without login credentials to use the built-in installer to attempt to reinstall a site.

That can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution, and the project rates the vulnerable configurations as uncommon. Fixed releases for all supported branches shipped yesterday.

The Drupal Security Team disclosed the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-132165, yesterday and rated it critical, 18 out of 25 on the project's risk scale.

The installer ships in every copy of Drupal core as the file /core/install.php and stays on the site after installation. Core's default .htaccess rules do not block requests to it, so blocking it is left to each site.

No attacks are reported in the security advisory, which rates exploitation as complex and records an existing proof-of-concept exploit. Some exploit paths are blocked where the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php.

The team had told site owners in an advance notice earlier this week to set aside time for the patch, warning that exploits may be developed within hours or days.

Every release below 10.6.22 is affected, along with Drupal 11 releases from 11.0.0 before 11.3.22 and from 11.4.0 before 11.4.13.

The fixed versions, detailed in the project's release notes, are:.

Sources indicate that the team recommends blocking the installer even after updating. Sites that cannot upgrade yet should follow the project's installer guidance, updated yesterday, which describes three options: a deny rule in the web server configuration, an .htaccess rule, or removing the file and keeping it removed with Composer scripts.

Sites that use the Drupal Steward protection service are already protected from known attack vectors, according to the team, and should still update in case upcoming vectors emerge.

Sources indicate that drupal 11.2.x and earlier, 10.5.x and earlier, and Drupal 8 and 9 are end-of-life and get no fix. The 11.3.x branch and Drupal 10 lose security coverage altogether in December under the project's support schedule.

In the week of November 8, 154,485 of the 528,430 sites reporting usage data to drupal.org, about 29 percent, were running end-of-life branches.

It has been revealed that the flaw was found by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, an automated service the AI tech giant launched on October 8 to look for vulnerabilities in open-source projects that opt in. Findings go to maintainers without human review, each with a reproducer and, where available, a candidate patch, according to its launch announcement.

Drupal's security team mentioned on November 2 that a surge of security reports, which it attributes to AI tools, is more than it can sustain at its current funding, and that it is cutting security coverage for core minor versions from 12 months to 8 starting in 2027.

This is the second critical remote code execution flaw fixed in Drupal core in two months, after the Field UI flaw patched on October 14, which also had at least one exploit path that needed no login.

  • In a recent development, the manual's own example is 5C 02 11 EC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A free-running rangefinder gives you a lot of numbers and no promises. The LRF50H, one of our 905 nm modules, streams 4-byte 5C frames at 1 kHz by default, so a flight controller or a PLC sees a newly introduced distance every millisecond. Most of them are fine. A few are not, and the few that are not tend to be the ones that matter.

I am Tommy Yu, an engineer at ERDI TECH LTD, the manufacturer of these modules. This post is about the part after the checksum: how I decide whether a decoded 5C value should be used. The evidence comes from a bench capture our factory recorded on 2026-11-06 for the ArduPilot driver work (ArduPilot/ardupilot#34983). Everything below was checked against the model documents and that capture on 2026-11-18.

In a recent development, the manual's own example is 5C 02 11 EC. The unit depends on the model, not on the family:.

So 5C 02 11 EC is 43.54 m on an H module and 4.354 m on a VB module. Reading the wrong row is a factor of ten.

In a recent development, the checksum is one byte. It catches most line noise, not all of it. A frame that passes was probably received as sent, which is a weaker statement than "the distance is right".

I keep these separate, because each one points at a different problem:.

Class 3 is the one people forget. The factory's LRF50H log, taken against a wall 1.9 m away, has 2000 frames. 1997 of them read between 189 and 204 cm (median 196 cm). Three read 31496, 36977 and 39688, which is 315, 370 and 397 m, on a module rated for 50 m. None of them is the 0xFFFF marker. The vendor tool accepted all three.

It has been revealed that I cannot tell you why. The log holds decoded values, not raw bytes, so I cannot say whether the module emitted them or whether corrupted frames happened to pass a one-byte checksum. What I can say is what they do to a naive consumer. Two of the three, at log positions 867 and 875, are eight frames apart. If your consumer averages the last nine frames, the second spike lands in a window that already holds the first one. I computed that mean over this log: it reaches 77.6 m while the wall has not moved.

It has been revealed that the rule I use is blunt: anything above the configured maximum is dropped and counted. The ArduPilot driver takes the same view and treats any frame beyond RNGFNDx_MAX as out-of-range instead of averaging it.

Do not use the datasheet's best-case range as the gate. LRF50H is specified to 50 m at 90% reflectivity and 15 m at 10%. A dark target at 20 m is a legitimate reading, and a gate set at 15 m would remove it. Set the gate at the largest number your application can legitimately see, such as the 50 m rating.

It has been revealed that A gate removes impossible values. A median removes the possible-but-wrong ones the gate cannot see. I keep the last nine frame slots, including the invalid ones, and only output a value when at least five of those slots are valid. Two consequences:.

On the replay, the median alone also handles those three spikes, because none of them sits in a run longer than four. What it did not do is make the signal quieter. The standard deviation of the valid frames was 2.73 cm and of the filtered output 2.73 cm. The log changes value only 56 times in 2000 lines, and the 189 to 204 cm spread is the module's real scatter at that wall. A median is an outlier filter, not a smoother. If you need smoothing, add it separately and accept its lag; our note on upgrade rate on moving platforms covers what a filter costs on a moving vehicle.

According to recent reports, size the window in time, not in frames. The tool that wrote the log recorded about 91 frames per second for the H module and about 94 for the VB module, and the factory notes say that rate comes from the tool's receive loop, not from the module. Nine slots are 9 ms if your host reads every frame at 1 kHz, and about 99 ms at 91 frames per second.

Recent findings suggest that the four counters are the useful output. Log them once a second. A rising skipped_bytes rate is a wiring problem and indicates up earlier than a wrong distance does. A rising beyond_max with a clean skipped_bytes is the pattern in the factory log.

I ran these before pasting, in a Python script with assertions:.

I have not run this against a live module or a raw byte capture. The factory log is the best evidence we have, and it is decoded values only. A raw capture and a flight-controller log are still the missing pieces for the claim "tested on hardware".

At 460800 baud a 4-byte frame is 40 bit times, so the line can carry 11,520 frames per second. 1 kHz uses about 8.7% of it. The parser is not where you will run out of time.

According to recent reports, if you have a raw hex capture of 20 or more frames that includes a bad one, send it to tommy@erdimail.com with the model name. I can say more from bytes than from a plot.

It has been revealed that disclosure: I am Tommy Yu, an engineer at ERDI TECH LTD (erdilrf.com), the manufacturer of the modules discussed. Data checked against our model documents and the 2026-11-06 factory bench capture on 2026-11-18.

Luhn and IBAN check digits explained: validating card numbers and bank accounts in Python

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (447 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A check digit is an extra digit computed from the others, so a typo makes the number invalid.
  • Working from the right, skip the check digit, double the next, skip one, double the next, and so on.
  • def luhn_valid(number: str) -> bool: digits = [int(c) for c in number if c.isdigit()] if len(digits) < 2 or re.search(r"[^\d\s-]", number): return False total = 0 for i, d in enumerate(reversed(digits)): if i % 2 == 1: # every second digit from the right, starting left of the check digit d *= 2 if d > 9: d -= 9 total += d return total % 10 == 0.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A check digit is an extra digit computed from the others, so a typo makes the number invalid. Card numbers use the Luhn algorithm: double every second digit from the right, subtract 9 from any result above 9, add everything up, and the total must end in 0. IBANs use mod 97: move the first four characters to the end, turn letters into numbers (A = 10 … Z = 35), and the result divided by 97 must leave a remainder of 1. Both catch typos before you call a payment API. Neither tells you the card or account exists. Here's tested Python for both, and what each one misses.

Take 7992739871 with check digit 3. Working from the right, skip the check digit, double the next, skip one, double the next, and so on. Doubled digits above 9 lose 9 (8 × 2 = 16 → 7). The sum of all digits, including the check digit, is 70, a multiple of 10, so the number is valid.

```python title="checkdigits.py: Luhn" import re.

def luhn_valid(number: str) -> bool: digits = [int(c) for c in number if c.isdigit()] if len(digits) < 2 or re.search(r"[^\d\s-]", number): return False total = 0 for i, d in enumerate(reversed(digits)): if i % 2 == 1: # every second digit from the right, starting left of the check digit d *= 2 if d > 9: d -= 9 total += d return total % 10 == 0.

def luhn_check_digit(partial: str) -> int: return next(d for d in range(10) if luhn_valid(partial + str(d))).

luhn_valid("4111 1111 1111 1111") # True, a well-known test card number luhn_valid("4111 1111 1111 1112") # False luhn_check_digit("7992739871") # 3.

It also can't catch a completely wrong but valid-looking number. One in ten random numbers passes.

An IBAN is a two-letter country code, two check digits, then the national account number (the BBAN). The check is the mod 97-10 scheme from ISO 7064:.

```python title="checkdigits.py: IBAN" IBAN_LENGTHS = {"DE": 22, "GB": 22, "PK": 24, "AE": 23, "SA": 24, "FR": 27, "NL": 18} # excerpt.

Recent findings suggest that def iban_valid(iban: str) -> bool: iban = re.sub(r"\s+", "", iban).upper() if not re.fullmatch(r"[A-Z]{2}\d{2}[A-Z0-9]+", iban): return False if IBAN_LENGTHS.get(iban[:2], len(iban)) != len(iban): return False rearranged = iban[4:] + iban[:4] as_digits = "".join(str(int(c, 36)) for c in rearranged) # A=10 ... Z=35 return int(as_digits) % 97 == 1.

def iban_check_digits(country: str, bban: str) -> str: as_digits = "".join(str(int(c, 36)) for c in bban + country + "00") return f"{98 - int(as_digits) % 97:02d}".

iban_valid("GB82 WEST 1234 5698 7654 32") # True, the standard example iban_valid("GB82 WEST 1234 5698 7654 33") # False iban_check_digits("DE", "370400440532013000") # '89'.

The PHP Foundation has released security updates to address multiple critical security flaws that could be exploited to achieve remote code execution on affected deployments, including CVE-2026-115560.

The list of vulnerabilities is as follows -.

Depthfirst, which has codenamed CVE-2026-126714 "phpAfterShell," has described it as a critical flaw that can enable a remote attacker to run arbitrary code on affected servers.

It has been revealed that "If a pwrite()/ftruncate() update is interrupted, PHP may leave behind a malformed session file that is later loaded by session_start(), yielding an arbitrary deserialization primitive," Depthfirst remarked. "Chained with another of our PHP-native deserialization-to-RCE findings, this leads directly to remote code execution.".

In a recent development, it affects any application that runs an affected PHP version with file-based sessions. If immediate patching is not possible, it's advised to turn off session upload progress.

Patches for the flaws are available in the following versions -.

Consumers who are using existing 8.2.x, 8.3.x, 8.4.x, and 8.5.x versions of PHP are advised to update to the latest version for optimal protection.

EU Digital Fairness Act Proposal Targets Dark Patterns in Online Shopping and Marketing

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Commission has proposed a Digital Fairness Act that would make fake scarcity messages, countdown-style pressure tactics and other manipulative online design practices a central target of EU consumer law.
  • It has been revealed that released on 11 November 2026, the Commission's formal Proposal for a Digital Fairness Act is intended to replace the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive with a regulation.
  • The proposal is not simply about individual checkout messages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Commission has proposed a Digital Fairness Act that would make fake scarcity messages, countdown-style pressure tactics and other manipulative online design practices a central target of EU consumer law. For online retailers, subscription businesses and marketing teams, the proposal is an important signal that conversion flows built around urgency, opaque pricing or difficult cancellation could face a more consistent regulatory standard across the EU.

It has been revealed that released on 11 November 2026, the Commission's formal Proposal for a Digital Fairness Act is intended to replace the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive with a regulation. That change matters because a regulation would be directly applicable across the EU if adopted, rather than relying on separate national transposition of a directive.

The proposal is not simply about individual checkout messages. It is a broad attempt to update consumer protection for digital markets, where interface design, personalisation and subscription mechanics can influence how people spend money and attention. The Commission frames the measure as part of its 2030 Consumer Agenda and 2026 work programme, with stronger consumer protections and a more level playing field for businesses as intended outcomes.

At its core, the Digital Fairness Act proposal would address dark patterns, meaning interface and marketing techniques that steer consumers through manipulation rather than clear, informed choice. The Commission specifically identifies false signals of demand or limited availability, such as claims that only a few products remain or that an offer is about to expire when those claims are not genuine.

The proposal also reaches beyond scarcity prompts. Its measures include:.

These provisions are proposed rules, not requirements already in force. Still, the detail in the Commission's text gives businesses a practical basis for reviewing the customer journeys most likely to be affected, especially product pages, cart and checkout steps, promotional emails, queueing systems and cancellation paths.

Industry observers note that many digital growth tactics are not inherently unfair. A genuine sale deadline, accurate inventory information and an optional subscription can all help consumers make decisions. The glitch is whether the presentation is truthful, understandable and leaves room for a meaningful choice.

Sources indicate that for example, a retailer that displays inventory based on real stock data is in a different position from one that permanently shows a low-stock warning to create pressure. Similarly, a countdown linked to a real promotion may differ from a timer that resets for every visitor. The proposal's focus on dark patterns puts the design and factual basis of those claims under greater scrutiny.

It has been revealed that the proposed move from a directive to a regulation is significant. The existing Unfair Commercial Practices Directive establishes EU-wide principles, but directives require implementation through national law. The Commission's proposed regulation is intended to reduce differences created by national transposition and support more harmonised enforcement across the Digital Single Market.

According to recent reports, the proposal also envisages enhanced, centralised enforcement through an amended Consumer Protection Cooperation framework. For companies operating in more than one EU country, a more harmonised regime could reduce the need to interpret substantially different national implementations. It could also make it more crucial to establish consistent website, campaign and subscription practices across markets.

That does not mean every business needs to redesign its entire digital presence now. The useful near-term step is to identify claims and interfaces that depend on urgency, obscured choices or cancellation friction. A documented review can distinguish legitimate promotional design from tactics that may become difficult to defend under the proposed framework.

Industry observers note that for smaller teams, this work is often less about adding latest software than about connecting the systems already in use. Inventory feeds need to support stock messages, promotion tools need reliable end dates, and subscription platforms need cancellation experiences that match what customers were promised. Marketing, ecommerce and customer support teams should be able to explain the customer journey in the same terms.

What is the EU Digital Fairness Act?

The Digital Fairness Act is a European Commission proposal released on 11 November 2026. It is intended to replace the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive with a directly applicable EU regulation focused on unfair digital practices, including dark patterns.

Would the proposal ban fake low-stock claims and countdown timers?

Industry observers note that the proposal explicitly targets manipulative marketing tactics, including fake scarcity claims such as false low-stock or limited-time messages. Commission materials also highlight countdown-style tactics as an example of the practices being addressed.

Is the Digital Fairness Act already in force?

No. The supplied Commission material describes a legislative proposal. Its measures would apply only if the proposal is adopted as an EU regulation.

What should an online store review first?

Review scarcity and deadline claims, price disclosures, online queue pricing, subscription renewal terms, cancellation flows, influencer disclosures and any personalised advertising or pricing that targets minors.

In a recent development, the Digital Fairness Act proposal would place a clearer boundary around digital tactics that turn consumer choice into pressure or confusion. Its eventual legal outcome remains to be determined, but the Commission's direction is clear: truthful claims, transparent pricing and straightforward cancellation are becoming central expectations for digital customer experiences.

Fun Fact: WebRTC renders audio (and video) based on when it arrives, not when it is supposed to be rendered. Every other protocol uses timestamps, but Mr. WebRTC barely looks at them, because accuracy is a non-goal. Sure, itâll nudge audio and video into sync by a few milliseconds, but good luck sending the video 500ms after the audio.

This is a huge problem for voice AI. TTS is generated faster than real-time, stamping each packet with a future timestamp. But in order to play back audio at the correct time with WebRTCâ¦ the agent needs to sleep before transmitting each packet.

Fuck that noise, MoQ supports multiple latency targets with a single connection. In the case of voice AI:.

Your real-time model can have a maximum latency of 500ms while your more accurate model might have a maximum latency of 5s. Both get coalesced into a single upstream subscription which can fanout.

And note that this is the maximum latency. The latency is 0 except during terrible network conditions, and eventually we give up. This is the core difference between MoQ and TCP/WebSocket for Voice AI.

Your transport latency should be aligned with your product latency budget.

Recent findings suggest that webRTC (and Opus) include Forward Error Correction to help mask packet loss. The idea is to stuff a crappier, lower bitrate copy of the previous audio frame into the next packet.

But only a single last packet. It canât even handle two lost packets in a row, let alone a full network blip.

It has been revealed that this is fine for WebRTC because it doesnât give a shit about audio older than 30ms. But itâs not fine for voice AI or really anything on the internet. Packet loss due to congestion is bursty, not random.

Recent findings suggest that A common âfixâ is to spread these copies over time, so you can handle X lost packets in a row. See Opus 1.5. All of this extra data has a real cost, and if you donât know what youâre doing (and you donât), then you will aggravate bufferbloat.

Industry observers note that in my humble (and attractive) opinion, FEC is best for huge RTTs, like transmitting to le moon. In , we instead use CDNs to shrink the lossy first/last mile which makes retransmissions OP. Why send more bytes spread over 400ms, instead of retransmitting in 40ms?

But if a WebRTC warrior insists, QUIC libraries can retransmit stream data as many times as they want. Basically RED but based on byte offsets, not packets, and fully transparent to the receiver. Thatâs a free idea btw.

💡 Key Takeaways
