That is what we set out to achieve. That was a feature table. That feature table is built by another fact log or an immutable log. This is just the searches that have happened over a period of time. By looking at this, it is just very clear that there is one data frame and the other data frame. We figured out we can actually just use Spark ML transformer, which did the feature translation between.

This is how it looked in its entirety. There were immutable fact logs, which is just log of search events that have happened in the past. We asked people to write reusable feature encoders that converted into a feature table. Once we had that, all anybody has to do is just go look at the initial dataset and do a time-wise join on it. We tried to do something similar to online as well. There were event streams. We asked people to write feature mappers in Scala, and that became enriched streams. From there, there was a centralized team which took all these features, put it into Cassandra, and then served it via an API. There were a couple of problems with this approach. One was parity. Data was different between online and offline. The computation was different from online and offline. Then there were performance issues because of the amount of data that we were processing in offline.

Industry observers note that backfilling or recomputation was hard. In the second attempt, we decided, let's fix data and computational parity together. The way we fixed data parity was we introduced the concept of timelines. Timelines is nothing but a time-ordered sequence of events for a user. User searched, user clicked, user booked, things like that. The idea was, let's build this timeline equally or approximately in the same way for both online and offline. Then that way, once we have that, we can just write computation once and then use the timeline. That was a big picture. This is how the timelines were built. Those are the search, clicks, and immutable events. They got materialized into Hadoop. We built timeline builders separately. It's a duplicate effort, but it was managed by a central team. That timeline was operating separately for online and offline. They synced the data or the timelines into Cassandra and HDFS. The only difference between these two timelines were the Cassandra timelines were trimmed. Unlike the MVA, TVA, we actually didn't trim timelines for saving the universe. We trimmed timelines in Cassandra for saving the space.

This is how we used timelines for computational parity. We had a full timeline in HDFS, a trimmed timeline in Cassandra. We asked people to write centralized shared feature libraries. These are things that can be used to compute features, things like sum, count, large scale, and all those typical things was written by a centralized team. It also allowed extension. Anybody could come in and write in the feature that is not already there. In online or in real time, when an application wanted some inference, they would go to a feature store API and ask, can you give me this feature? What it would do is go into Cassandra, pick up the timeline for that specific user or use case, and then build that feature on the fly with these shared libraries. The same happened on the training side or on offline. That stack was Python, because scientists were using Python.

We had a wrapper, which had a feature computation library wrapper. What it did was, whenever the scientist wanted a feature, it submitted a Spark job. In that Spark job, we actually did the same thing. We typically achieved what we wanted to do, both data and feature parity. The problem was, ML scientists were not familiar with writing features in Java, and that created a dependency between engineering and ML science. Secondly, in the previous one, the Cassandra timelines, computing features on the fly was costly, expensive, because it took more than 90 milliseconds or so to actually just fetch the data. It was not suitable for most of the use cases. Then we said, ok, third attempt. Forget feature computation, we'll just focus on feature storage and serving. Let people deal with feature computation. We didn't care how features are computed, as long as we knew where to pick the features from.

If it was pre-computed, ok, we'll go to a data lake of sorts. If it is real time, we'll go to Kafka. Then we built a feature store. In the feature store, there was an ingestor component, which knew about these multiple data sources, and pulled that data, and stored it into an online store, and served it via an API. In this API, there was no on-the-fly computation. It was just a simple lookup, because features were already computed. The same pipeline, what it also did was sync data into offline, so that MLS can use it for retraining purposes, and for also other analysis. This feature store also had other benefits, like it had feature registry, feature monitoring, and so on. In essence, after three attempts, this is what we learned. It's a multidimensional problem, and we don't have an answer. Currently, for the pre-computation and real time, we currently have three systems, and we are always looking for one more system. That wraps the second layer.

Now in that third layer, we are moving away from infrastructure to business impact. I want to give you a high-level tour of all the ML platforms that we have, and then dive into one of them. This is the platform that we have. One is GenAI platform. It's the newest kid in the block. What it does is it enables any team to actually safely build generative AI experiences. It provides tools and infrastructure and foundational capabilities like guardrails, evaluation, orchestration out of the box. Things like PII detection, PII masking, everything comes out of the box. The product teams can focus just on product innovation and not on LLM plumbing. Let's look at a few use cases there, what we have. The trip planning, which is just a conversational experience where someone can go talk in natural language and get recommendations, that's powered by GenAI. We have smart filters.

Sources indicate that if you were ever on Booking.com, you would see hundreds of filters on the left, and it is hard for anyone to know which to pick. We have a text box where you can type it, and that translated into the right filters and sorters. The third is review summaries. That provides, based on the last reviews, a quick snapshot of pros and cons. The next is property Q&A. This actually enables instant answers to any property-specific questions, and it is grounded on reviews, past Q&A, and that is also powered by GenAI. We also have a booking support, wherein we have AI that can do basic customer support on payments, cancellation, and things regarding your booking. These are the use cases. There are many interesting things under the platform, but we are not going to cover it today.

GenAI is good, but to generate data, we actually want good content. That's where content intelligence comes in. What it does is it provides surfaces like good, high-quality content that are usable. This platform analyzes every image and text. It actually adds metadata or enriches that metadata. For example, if it is images, it adds themes, tags, and looks for any harmful content. If it is text, it looks for, for example, sentiments or topics that have been discussed. This also supports the reviews. Because most of the things happen in the background, like fraud detection is also taken care of by this content intelligence. One example that you see, anytime you see a gallery on Booking.com, it is probably powered by this content intelligence. Picking up the right photo to put up front and the order, which photos to highlight and so on. The other thing is, it autogenerates all text for screen readers.

There's a platform for that. It also does reviews. It detects topics on the reviews and summarizes it at the property level. This is what it enabled was, not just getting intelligence at content level, but going one level higher. For example, if property had all the images and all the summaries, we can actually create intelligence at the property level to see what is happening. That kind of aggregation level, this platform enabled. The third is ranking. Ranking's responsibility is to order millions of products so that any time a customer comes in, they see the most relevant results for them, like something personalized. This is a platform that we are going to dig in, so I'll park it here. Recommendations is a self-serve platform wherein you can build any kind of recommendations across the funnel, from discovery to post-booking. It has more than 40, 50 use cases. I picked a few to give you a flavor of what it looks like.

The pushcards that you might see on Booking.com is powered by recommendations. There's multi-vertical recommendations. When I say multi-vertical, I'm referring to accommodations, flights, attractions, and so on. Those kinds of recommendations come from this platform. Unique stays, team-based recommendations for you, and attraction carousels that you might see on the page, and any flight recommendations. All of these are examples that are powered by recommendations platform. The last platform is value intelligence. The responsibility of this platform is to measure and optimize promotions. By promotions, I mean anything like vouchers, discounts, things like rewards that's being optimized by value intelligence. The goal of this platform is to say, maximize value for travelers, partners, and the business. That wraps all the platforms.

According to recent reports, let's jump into ranking platform. Ranking is a three-way optimization problem. We need choice and value for customers. We need exposure and growth for the partners. We also need efficiency and revenue for business. If we show irrelevant results, the travelers are going to be annoyed. If we show poor visibility, partners are going to be frustrated. If any one of them is annoyed for too long, I'm going to get my salary re-ranked. It's a three-way optimization problem. Back then in 2005, we had the formula for ranking hotels look like this. It was simple. It was just a simple function, which took bookings and views, and a random tiebreaker in case there were two hotels which had the same rank. The formula evolved over time. We introduced cancellations. It was taking consideration of seasonality. What is the distance of the hotel from the center? What is the number of views the hotel is getting?

In a recent development, availability of the hotel. The average ranking in the locality. What is the visitor traffic? Guest reviews. These are just some flavors of what are the factors we considered. Back then, ranking actually was computed offline using simple Perl cron scripts every night, and then the scores were dumped into MySQL, and we used it in real time. Around 2016, we actually tried to replace the ranking formula with machine learning, and we failed miserably. The handcrafted formula was undefeatable. We could not beat it for a long time, like one and a half years or so. This formula cannot be beaten. The reasons were many fold. The primary reason was that the ideal model that we wanted to train the model on, and the massive amount of data that we had was not actually helpful when Spark kept exploding. The memory of Spark was not sufficient. What we did was we cut corners, we made some approximations, and we succeeded. In true Booking sense, we ran an experiment, and it was successful.

Industry observers note that next, we wanted to tackle personalized ranking, and there was a problem. This is what it looked like. The ranking scores was calculated offline until then. It was put into MySQL, and an availability engine read that MySQL data, loaded it into memory. The responsibility of this availability engine was that it needs to search the availability and prices of millions of properties. Because of the amount of data that this engine had, it used a scatter-gather pattern. It had a coordinator and 24 shards. Each of those shards actually worked on a subset of the data. When a request came in from the user, it came to the availability engine via a search orchestrator, and the request landed there. The request contained something like this. Where does the user want to search on? When? Then, what is the party size? Then, what are the filters and preferences of the user?

Industry observers note that the coordinator accepted that request and then distributed the work to the workers. Workers went on to do their job. They actually looked into the subset of the data that they had, took the data out, and then they used the ranking scores that were preloaded into memory to do the sorting. After they did the sorting, they supplied the results back to the coordinator. Coordinator aggregated all the information from the workers and re-sorted the results and gave the results back to the search. This is what was happening. If you wanted to personalize, meaning that every user gets a specific set of results, what we had to do was take the ranking logic out of this availability engine, get rid of those static scores at the bottom, and then replace it with a service. Then have that service invoke actually a model which is deployed in the model serving platform that we saw earlier.

That's what we wanted to do. There were two problems. The first problem was, if there were 1,000 requests for the availability engine, it meant that the new service is going to get 24,000 requests because it was sitting behind the fanout, behind the shards. Secondly, the availability engine was operating at super low latency, and that also meant that this new service plus the network hop to the model and the model's time all needs to be well within the time of that service. It's basically a high throughput, low latency problem, and we managed to crack it. These are the numbers from 2024. That ranking service that you saw in the previous slide, that green box that was introduced new, is able to solve 100,000 requests per second with a p99.9 latency of 100 milliseconds. The average is way low. It's like 40, 50 milliseconds or so.

I want to share one more thing before I wrap up the evolution story. Experiments at Booking typically run for two to four weeks, but this meant that we couldn't actually train or run models. We were limited in the number of models that we can run every year, because we just had 53 weeks. We wanted to move faster, knowing well that if we actually put in a bad ranking model upfront, it is going to cost all of us, like travelers, partners, and business. What we did was we introduced interleaving. This is how it worked. Typically, for an A/B testing, we actually take the people and split them across two groups, and then we show different search results for them, which was coming from different ranking models. In interleaving, what we did was we didn't show two groups, we didn't split the groups, we just revealed the same results for all users.

In a recent development, those results were coming from merged data, meaning we would train a couple of models, in this case, two models, red and blue. We trained the model, and each of these models gave a list of results. Then we would somehow need to merge it. One simple example could be, take the top one from here, top one from here, merge it. Then keep alternating it. It's just a team draft approach. Then once you have done, you present that to all users across the service. Then you check offline, ok, from which list did the user interact more? Was it from model A or from model B? That gives us the answer. Why it was useful was we could suddenly run more variants. On the right side, it doesn't have to be two. We can even run eight different models that are actually interleaving the results for search. That is, we can run more variants that was like 10 times speed-up than what we are used to with A/B testing.

Sources indicate that we could use it with less traffic because interleaving is super sensitive to customer preferences, and we can get signals faster. The way we use it now, interleaving and A/B, is that we train a bunch of models, we pre-select it with interleaving, we pick up a winner, and then we take the winner and then do proper A/B testing. We have optimized both speed, while not losing scientific rigor.

It has been revealed that I started the talk by saying that experiment laid the foundation in general for data-driven decision-making. You can see that, still, it continues to underpin what we do every day. With that, that concludes the evolution story.

Industry observers note that next, I want to tell you where we are going. These are the five platforms that you saw. What we started doing last year is that we started building the foundations of agentic systems. By agentic systems, think about memories, all kinds of memories, episodic, semantic, procedural, and think about agent serving, like access control for those agents, delegation controls for the consumers to those agents, agent-to-agent communication. Those are the things we started working on last year. Parallelly, what we are also doing is unifying all these platforms under a single umbrella and then having a single orchestration layer. Why? Because we foresee a possible fragmentation and we wanted to avoid it earlier. Like for cross-domain use cases, we want a single, centralized, unified experience for the customer, and this platform can do that. Secondly, we wanted to centralize all kinds of AI-related governance, security, quality, and all those things. We wanted to centralize that.

Sources indicate that agents differ here. Some start from a blank URL and rebuild the map on every run. Others start from an existing model of your site and keep it current between runs. Ask which one you're buying, what carries over between runs, and whether the agent keeps discovering beyond its starting map. A starting map should be a head start, not a boundary.

It has been revealed that without context, an AI agent behaves like a smart scanner. With context, it can reason about your application. That changes what it finds, not just how fast. When a security researcher hunted for flaws in Apache Airflow, their AI assistant called the search a dead end. Testing how the deployment’s parts trust each other, instead of reading the code, turned up an unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2026-68982).

In a recent development, A suspicious pattern is not an exploitable vulnerability. Ask whether the agent exploits what it suspects, reproduces its findings, and hands over evidence your team can verify. A list of suspected concerns is not a validated pentest.

Here is what proof looks like. During an authorized assessment of a major insurer's production website, an AI pentesting agent found that the one-time passcode request could send login codes to any email address. It proved the flaw by logging in with a code sent to its own inbox, and guardrails then stopped the test. The insurer said it had pentested the site about six months earlier (Reflectiz case study on The Hacker News).

A demo can look convincing without proving that the agent reaches your logged-in workflows, validates what it finds, or confirms your fixes. Here are three of the 15 checks to run before you choose.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (637 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • claude-mem is a free, open-source tool that gives your coding agent a memory across sessions.
  • The project lives at thedotmack/claude-mem on GitHub.
  • claude-mem hooks into your coding agent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

claude-mem is a free, open-source tool that gives your coding agent a memory across sessions. A coding agent is a program that writes and edits code for you from plain prompts. Each upcoming session starts blank. The agent re-reads the same files, re-asks the same questions, and repeats mistakes you already fixed. claude-mem records what happens in each session, and it hands the key facts to the next session.

The project lives at thedotmack/claude-mem on GitHub. It holds more than 118,000 stars, and it uses the Apache-2.0 license. The current release is version 16.0.0, published 18 November 2026.

claude-mem hooks into your coding agent. A hook is a small step that runs when a set event starts or ends. The hooks watch SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, and SessionEnd. Each event sends the tool activity to a small local worker on your machine. A second agent, called the observer, turns that activity into short notes. When a session ends, the observer writes a summary.

The next session opens with a short index of past notes. It pulls full details only when it needs them. Your memory lives in a folder named .claude-mem in your home folder. The notes sit in a local database file, and a search index helps the agent find old work fast. The agent can also search your history in three steps: find an index entry, view the timeline around it, and fetch the full note. You can also run /learn-codebase to front-load a whole repo, which takes about five minutes on a typical repo.

Run one command in your terminal: npx claude-mem install. The installer finds the coding agents on your machine, and it asks which ones to set up. Then restart Claude Code. Your second session in a project opens with memory from the first. To test it, do real work in one session, close it, and open a newly introduced session in the same project. Ask the agent what you decided last time.

If it recalls the choice, the memory works. You need Node.js 20.19 or later, or Node.js 22.12 or later. The installer adds Bun and uv itself when they are missing. Do not use npm install -g claude-mem. That command installs the library only. It does not set up the hooks or start the worker.

The project indicates the observer runs off-plan, so you get up to 100 percent more use from your plan. Treat that number as the project claim, not a test result. Anonymous use data is on by default, and you can turn it off with npx claude-mem telemetry disable. Tool screenshots stay on your machine by default, and they upload only when cloud sync is on. Your memory stays local unless you turn cloud sync on. Wrap text in tags to keep it out of memory.

One caution from the project history: in late October 2026, a user report mentioned the installer sent 30 days of prompts to the project server. The report said this happened without asking first. That report is now closed, and the current installer asks you to choose each option. Read the setup screens with care before you accept them.

Industry observers note that claude-mem solves a real pain: every coding session starts blank, and re-teaching the agent costs time. One command sets it up, and the memory stays on your machine unless you choose cloud sync. The trial asks for a payment method, so set a reminder before day 30 if you do not proposal to pay. The privacy history demonstrates why you should read each setup screen.

In a recent development, if you use Claude Code each day, try it on one project first. Watch the second session. If the agent recalls your last choice, keep it.

#445. Repurposing long recordings: what it takes to get 3–5 usable vertical clips

Repurposing long recordings: what it takes to get 3–5 usable vertical clips

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (621 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, most creators already own the raw material for short-form video.
  • I have been building FreeClipping around that problem, and this post is about the pipeline decisions that mattered more than the model choices.
  • Transcription is a solved-ish commodity now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, most creators already own the raw material for short-form video. It is sitting in a webinar recording, a podcast episode, or a 40-minute interview. The hard part is not filming more. It is finding the eight or ten seconds inside forty minutes that will actually hold attention on a vertical feed.

I have been building FreeClipping around that problem, and this post is about the pipeline decisions that mattered more than the model choices.

Transcription is a solved-ish commodity now. Whisper-class models give you word-level timestamps for a fraction of a cent per minute, and the quality on clear English speech is good enough that captioning is no longer the bottleneck.

What breaks a clipping tool is choosing which moments to cut. Two failure modes show up constantly:.

The fix I settled on is boring: score candidate windows, then do constrained non-overlapping selection over the ranked list, and snap boundaries to sentence edges from the transcript before rendering. The clips get slightly shorter than the naive window, and dramatically more watchable.

In a recent development, cropping a 16:9 frame to 9:16 is lossy by definition. There is no crop that keeps a two-person interview, a slide, and burned-in captions all legible. Every tool picks a lane:.

Sources indicate that freeClipping renders 9:16 MP4 with burned-in captions on a simple background. Captions are burned in rather than delivered as a sidecar file because the target platforms reward on-screen text and because a caption track that fails to load is worse than no caption at all.

Audio-only sources get the same treatment: the waveform becomes a captioned video on a plain background. Podcasters get vertical clips without ever turning on a camera.

Video jobs take minutes, not milliseconds. If the only feedback is a spinner, users close the tab and assume it failed.

In a recent development, A persistent job URL solved this better than email notifications did. The job page shows status, and when it finishes the same URL is the download page for each clip. Users bookmark it, come back on their phone, and download. No account required, no magic link.

It has been revealed that retention is explicit rather than implied: sources and cached transcripts expire after seven days, generated clips after thirty. Saying that up front removes a whole category of support questions.

The first recording is free up to 10 minutes without an account or a card. That sounds generous until you notice it is one recording — enough to evaluate whether the highlight selection is any good on your own material, not enough to run a weekly show.

It has been revealed that later Free usage requires sign-in and includes 20 source minutes per calendar month per verified account, with watermarked 720p exports. Paid tiers are $9/month for 150 source minutes and $19/month for 500, with 1080p exports and no watermark.

Sources indicate that the sign-in requirement exists because per-account minutes need an account to attach to. It is not a growth funnel trick, and I would rather say that plainly than pretend otherwise.

In a recent development, get the non-overlapping selection logic right before you touch framing. Ship a persistent job URL before you ship notifications. Make retention limits visible in the UI. And measure the thing that matters — how many of the generated clips a creator actually posts — instead of how many clips the model generated.

If you want to try the pipeline on your own recording, FreeClipping is the product; the first ten minutes cost nothing and no account is needed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Cambridge Dictionary has named ‘human’ as the Word of the Year 2026.

The year has been defined by global debates on what it means to be human when AI is blurring the boundaries between people and machines.

'Human' is defined in the Cambridge Dictionary as ‘having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines’.

According to recent reports, in 2026, many public figures defended humans and humanity in the age of AI. Bill Gates, Chair of the Gates Foundation, made the case for “human reserved jobs”, such as caregivers, that should never be taken by machines, in a widely read essay.

Commenting on the selection of ‘human’ as Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year, he said: “AI is making us think harder about what it means to be human. It could help us cure diseases, improve education, and give people more time to spend on the things that matter most.

"But we need to make deliberate choices about how it fits into our lives, including where we want people to remain at the center. The measure of AI’s success should be how much it improves human lives.”.

In a recent development, ‘AI godfather’ and Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton has warned that “we’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans.” And in his Magnifica Humanitas letter, Pope Leo XIV spoke of newly introduced forms of “dehumanization” and the “pressing duty to remain profoundly human”.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Project Hail Mary author Andy Weir has wondered whether he "might be among the last generation of fully human writers". The Authors Guild has debuted a ‘Human Authored’ kitemark for books, supported by Professor Dame Mary Beard and Malorie Blackman.

In a recent development, as AI deepfakes simulated humans, Matthew McConaughey became the first Hollywood actor to pre-emptively protect himself against unauthorised digital reproduction by trademarking clips of his voice, his face and even his catchphrase ‘alright, alright, alright’. Taylor Swift followed suit, trademarking her voice and image in April.

Sources indicate that professor Rachel Adams, an expert on AI governance and human rights at the University of Cambridge, said: “AI brings us back to questions that we’ve asked for millennia: who are we, what does it mean to be human? The answer to these questions has never been fixed or stable, but the act of asking it is something we have in common.

Sources indicate that “AI is going to be a profound test for humanity. There’s a real risk that it deepens existing inequalities, but it also has the potential to solve them.".

Dr Tom McClelland, a philosopher of science at the University of Cambridge, stated: “I think ‘human’ is a really interesting choice because right now our understanding of humanity is changing.

According to recent reports, “We're trying to understand the difference between a human mind and an artificial mind, between living beings like us and artificial beings that we're creating. What sets us apart, is it consciousness, creativity or compassion?

#443. Latest Attack Bypasses TPM Lockout to Crack Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs in Days, Not Years

Latest Attack Bypasses TPM Lockout to Crack Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs in Days, Not Years

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1350 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thehackernews

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On AMD-based PCs and some Intel PCs, the TPM lockout for Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs can be reset by someone who opens the PC's case, researchers at Technische Universität Berlin say.
  • Recent findings suggest that that leaves short PINs open to guessing.
  • According to recent reports, both PINs were set by the researchers and found within 236 tries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On AMD-based PCs and some Intel PCs, the TPM lockout for Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs can be reset by someone who opens the PC's case, researchers at Technische Universität Berlin say.

Recent findings suggest that that leaves short PINs open to guessing. In lab tests, the researchers found a four-digit Hello PIN on an AMD laptop and a 6-digit BitLocker PIN on an Intel laptop this way.

According to recent reports, both PINs were set by the researchers and found within 236 tries. From the speeds they measured, they calculate a worst-case of 40 hours for a four-digit Hello PIN, compared to 69 days with the lockout working as documented. For a default six-digit BitLocker PIN, the worst-case time drops from 19 years to 20 days.

Industry observers note that AMD confirmed yesterday that its processor firmware has a flaw that allows the attack on some PCs with its chips. It plans fixes for most of those chips between November and February 2027. For now, the researchers advise adding at least two digits to Hello and BitLocker PINs.

Recent findings suggest that the TPM in these PCs is a firmware TPM, built into the processor. Unlike a separate TPM chip, it has no secure storage of its own, according to the research paper the researchers posted late last week. So it keeps its saved state, including the count of wrong guesses, encrypted on the mainboard's flash chip.

If someone copies that saved state and later writes the old copy back, the count goes back too, unless the PC detects it. Newer PCs try to catch this with counters inside the flash chip, called RPMC, that can only go up.

In a recent development, on AMD PCs that use these counters, the processor's firmware never verifies that a counter actually increased. A small board placed between the processor and the flash chip can block the enhancement and report success, causing the PC to accept the old state.

RPMC chips from flash maker Winbond have a different weakness, the researchers found. A brief drop in the chip's power supply, called a voltage glitch, can cause the chip to reveal the secret key that signs its counter values. With that key, which took about a second to extract with their best settings, the board can forge any counter value.

On the Intel laptop they tested, one glitch was enough: the laptop's firmware feeds the chip the same value at every boot, so the leaked key kept working after each restart.

According to recent reports, for the Hello test, the researchers attacked a locked HP OmniBook 3 with an AMD Ryzen AI 5 330 processor and a BitLocker-encrypted drive. Their setup typed PINs from 1000 upward and reached the correct one, 1235, after 236 tries in 57 minutes.

Windows still forced a restart after every 5 incorrect PIN attempts on that laptop, but no lockout delay was applied. Microsoft's lockout defaults lock the TPM after 32 wrong tries and forget one failure every 10 minutes.

Sources indicate that the BitLocker test ran on a Framework Laptop 13 with an Intel Core Ultra 5 125H processor and Winbond flash. BitLocker's startup prompt adds no limit of its own, so each reset gave a fresh 32 tries. The setup found the PIN, 123457, after 236 tries in 6 minutes and 55 seconds.

In a recent development, in both tests, the researchers took the flash chip off the mainboard and wired in their own board. A script read the screen, typed PINs, and restarted the laptop through a KVM switch. They also changed firmware settings to slow each laptop's link to the flash chip, because their board could not keep up at full speed.

According to recent reports, the researchers make two further claims that their tests did not cover. Either method could be used against either PIN. A recovered Hello PIN can also unlock keys tied to the device and enable Hello-based single sign-on at work, and, in some configurations, pass a multi-factor check.

Industry observers note that the researchers have published their attack firmware, board designs, and scripts. They say reproducing the RPMC attacks is not plug-and-play and needs one of their boards. Neither the paper nor the vendor notices published so far describe attacks outside the lab.

Whether the attack works depends on the processor and the flash chip:.

The researchers expect the AMD firmware flaw to affect AMD PCs that use the Microsoft Pluton security core as their TPM, but did not show this.

On an AMD PC, the owner can boot Linux, for example from a live USB stick, and run the command grep . /sys/bus/pci/drivers/ccp/*/rpmc_* from the researchers' exposure check. The output indicates whether RPMC flash is present and enabled, which tells the owner which of the two methods applies. Missing files do not mean the PC lacks RPMC.

Industry observers note that for Intel PCs, the researchers know of no such check. Owners would have to open the PC and look for a Winbond chip marked 25R or 74M.

AMD tracks the flaw as CVE-2026-43613 and assigns it a CVSS score of 5.1 in a security bulletin published yesterday.

The chipmaker says attacks requiring physical access fall outside its product security threat model, but that "RPMC is intended to stop this type of interposer attack." The researchers first told it about the flaw in February.

The chipmaker's fix targets run from November to February 2027 across Ryzen, Ryzen AI, Ryzen Threadripper, Athlon and EPYC chips, and one unnamed product has no date yet. These are planned dates for its own firmware, not updates already out for PCs.

Recent findings suggest that the bulletin does not cover AMD PCs without RPMC flash. It also does not say whether the update will prevent an attacker from installing older, unfixed firmware on the PC, which the researchers say a fix must prevent.

Intel, whose processor was in the BitLocker test laptop, said in a security announcement earlier this week that the research "did not demonstrate a vulnerability in an Intel component". That matches the tests, in which the attack on the Intel laptop needed the Winbond chip's flaw.

According to the researchers, Intel's security team called the reused value a weakness rather than a vulnerability.

In a recent development, the researchers told Microsoft in April. According to them, the company rated the Windows Hello report as "moderate severity" and below its bar for an immediate fix, issued no CVE or bounty, and committed to raising its recommended minimum Hello PIN length to six digits.

It has been revealed that at the company's request, the researchers filed the BitLocker finding as a separate report for a different team. The company declined to give them any further written statement for the paper.

Separately, a Windows 11 test build released late last week makes six digits the minimum for personal-account Hello PINs, with an option to use four. The release notes give no reason, and features in that test channel may never reach regular releases.

According to the researchers, Winbond was first told about its chips' weakness to voltage glitches in January 2025 and received a second report in April showing that a glitch also leaks the key. The flash maker is studying the glitch, possibly including a new chip design, but has not committed to a fix or a date.

Two extra digits make a large difference in the researchers' figures:.

* BitLocker accepts a four-digit PIN only if an admin lowers the six-digit minimum. The times are worst cases calculated from speeds measured on one laptop each.

In May, Microsoft advised moving BitLocker from TPM-only to TPM+PIN to block the YellowKey bypass, as part of its YellowKey mitigation. The same TPM lockout guards that PIN.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, corporate cybersecurity expenditure operates under a deeply flawed thermodynamic model: organizational inertia resists movement until an external thermal shock injects the exact energy required to shift priorities. During stable periods, executive boards view security as an abstract, non-revenue-generating friction point—a dead weight on the operational balance sheet. Because digital safety yields no visible physical product during standard business cycles, leadership consistently underfunds preventative architecture.

According to recent reports, the mechanism of budget allocation changes instantly only when a catastrophic breach or system outage occurs. This crisis acts as a destructive kinetic impact on the corporate structure:.

Industry observers note that consequently, the post-incident window provides the sole viable operational vector for security leaders to secure capital expenditure. Boards transition from cost containment to emergency infrastructure hardening, systematically overriding prior inertia to fund long-overdue preventative controls.

Corporate cybersecurity spending historically operates under a reactive economic model: executive governance treats digital defense as an abstract operational overhead until a catastrophic breach materializes. This shock manifests as an acute systemic failure—materializing severe regulatory penalties, enterprise valuation contraction, and fiduciary liability—that instantly shatters board-level inertia and unlocks emergency capital. While destructive, this crisis mechanism paradoxically serves as the primary catalyst for securing long-overdue structural budgets. However, this panic-driven capital influx triggers a severe institutional paradox, fueling short-term hiring surges and reactive deployments that frequently degrade long-term system resilience.

When a major breach or high-profile infrastructure outage occurs, the sudden convergence of legal exposure and reputational damage forces an immediate reallocation of capital. Boards transition overnight from aggressive cost containment to unrestrained emergency defense spending. Yet, injecting capital into an active operational vacuum generates severe frictional costs across engineering and organizational workflows:.

Relying on post-incident crises to fund digital defense locks organizations into an unsustainable boom-and-bust cycle. As the immediate regulatory and public-relations shock dissipates, executive oversight wanes, fiscal discipline hardens into budget contraction, and bloated security units face attrition or dismantling. True strategic resilience requires decoupling risk mitigation from catastrophic triggers. Organizations must systematically embed continuous assurance, threat modeling, and preventative architecture into the core engineering lifecycle—transforming security from a volatile, crisis-driven reaction into an immutable operational invariant.

Industry observers note that to evaluate the structural trajectory of the cybersecurity job market, we must look past corporate public relations and analyze the mechanical failure modes of panic-driven funding. A major security breach functions as a violent kinetic shock that shatters executive inertia, paradoxically acting as the sole catalytic mechanism capable of unlocking long-overdue capital budgets. However, this emergency capital injection rarely funds graceful engineering; instead, it triggers a chaotic surge in headcount acquisition that strains organizational infrastructure akin to forcing high-voltage current through an unrated copper trace. The resulting thermal dissipation—manifested as administrative drag, tool sprawl, and catastrophic engineering burnout—dictates how talent demand fractures across four distinct operational trajectories.

Ultimately, the trajectory of cyber talent demand depends entirely on whether executive leadership continues to treat security as a volatile repair bill or embraces architectural resilience as an inviolable law of operational physics. Until organizations institutionalize preventative governance into their foundational layers, the job market will remain an inevitable captive of the next major outage.

Recent findings suggest that for too long, the cybersecurity industry has operated on a destructive metabolic loop: corporate inertia starves preventative engineering of capital until a catastrophic breach strikes, forcing a violent release of panic-driven funding. This boom-and-bust cycle does not build resilience; it fractures infrastructure. When a major incident hits, the sudden cash injection triggers a recursive hiring bottleneck. Organizations rapidly onboard unvetted personnel under inflated compensation packages, bypassing rigorous technical evaluations. These rushed hires deploy uncoordinated security tools and misconfigured access permissions directly onto legacy systems without cohesive threat modeling, creating identity conflicts and expanding the system's attack surface.

To decouple professional careers and organizational survival from sensationalized catastrophe cycles, security leaders must abandon the compliance treadmill and the permanent panic trap. Relying on statutory box-checking audits shifts technical bandwidth away from actual vulnerability remediation, locking teams into generating static PDF reports while active exploit vectors widen in unpatched dependencies. Similarly, leaning entirely on heuristic machine learning to automate defense creates cache saturation and analyst alert fatigue. When rigid, black-box AI scanners generate millions of low-fidelity alerts, human cognitive overload spikes, causing analysts to drop or misclassify critical anomalies and allowing multi-stage privilege-escalation paths to slip through unnoticed.

Breaking this volatile loop requires transitioning to continuous preventative governance. Organizations must integrate native threat modeling directly into the core software development lifecycle, shifting capital allocation from reactionary incident-response mercenaries to embedded application security architects. By treating security as a structural component of engineering rather than a post-hoc patch, companies eliminate memory corruptions, improper permission scopes, and unvetted code paths before deployment. This structural shift flattens out the volatility of the labor market, replacing emergency headcount surges and subsequent institutional brain drains with predictable, sustainable defense engineering.

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Krebsonsecurity

Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1156 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a manufacturer that helps websites customize user experiences and test out fresh features.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely.
  • Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a manufacturer that helps websites customize user experiences and test out fresh features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

Recent findings suggest that the Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.

Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.

Industry observers note that “The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”.

Contacted for comment, Optimizely mentioned that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”.

According to recent reports, “We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”.

According to recent reports, many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.

Sources indicate that one reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely demonstrates, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.

Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is notable since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.

“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he stated. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”.

Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.

In a recent development, “With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, latest domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”.

According to recent reports, how broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The manufacturer found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.

Sources indicate that the overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security complications. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.

Helme noted he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.

“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme remarked in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”.

Industry observers note that internet owners can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each upcoming website.

Sources indicate that happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?

Recent findings suggest that revision, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.

LinkedIn Cuts Daily Spark Shuffle Fetch Failures from 750 to 20 with Apache Celeborn

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News LinkedIn Cuts Daily Spark Shuffle Fetch Failures from 750 to 20 with Apache Celeborn.
  • Nov 18, 2026 2 min read.
  • LinkedIn has deployed Apache Celeborn as a shared remote shuffle platform across the majority of its Apache Spark and Apache Flink workloads, separating intermediate data storage from compute infrastructure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News LinkedIn Cuts Daily Spark Shuffle Fetch Failures from 750 to 20 with Apache Celeborn.

Nov 18, 2026 2 min read.

LinkedIn has deployed Apache Celeborn as a shared remote shuffle platform across the majority of its Apache Spark and Apache Flink workloads, separating intermediate data storage from compute infrastructure. The deployment reduces daily shuffle fetch failures from approximately 750 to 20, lowers compute costs by 10%, and improves application runtimes by 14%, compared with its previous Magnet implementation.

Daily shuffle fetch failures decreased from approximately 750 to 20 (Source: LinkedIn Blog Post).

LinkedIn's offline data platform executes more than 300,000 Spark jobs daily across thousands of production nodes, consuming approximately 200 petabyte-hours of compute. As the company moves toward a unified Flink architecture for real-time and historical processing, large-scale backfills introduce additional shuffle workloads. Shuffle moves intermediate data between processing stages, potentially stressing networks, disks, and application runtimes.

Industry observers note that linkedIn previously addressed shuffle read inefficiencies with Magnet, its push-based shuffle implementation contributed to Apache Spark 3.2. Magnet aggregates shuffle blocks by reducer partition into larger files, reducing random disk reads. However, shuffle storage remained within the compute cluster, where External Shuffle Services shared CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network resources with compute workloads.

In a recent development, with Apache Celeborn, map tasks push intermediate data to dedicated workers, which aggregate and store partitions independently of compute executors. Reducers fetch the data directly from these workers, allowing shuffle storage to scale independently of compute and reducing dependence on executor lifecycles. Unlike Magnet, which uses merger External Shuffle Services within the Spark compute cluster, Celeborn runs as a separate shuffle service with dedicated workers and a replicated control plane. This separation reduces resource contention between compute and shuffle workloads.

Celeborn architecture at LinkedIn (Source: LinkedIn Blog Post).

Aravind Patnam, a staff software engineer at LinkedIn, explained,.

Operating it reliably across thousands of nodes and hundreds of thousands of daily applications required substantial engineering beyond the upstream project.

It has been revealed that the deployment uses a five-node Raft-based control plane distributed across availability zones, with Apache Ratis providing metadata replication, leader election, and failover. LinkedIn also introduced network-aware replication and integrated Celeborn with its host health platform to deprioritize workers approaching maintenance and exclude degraded workers. These changes contributed to a 20-fold reduction in task failures during infrastructure disruptions compared with Magnet.

LinkedIn further optimized the data plane by moving shuffle storage to NVMe SSDs, reducing overall shuffle duration by 40%. Using Zstandard compression instead of LZ4 reduced the required shuffle worker fleet by approximately 35%. The tech giant also provisioned workers with 100 Gbps network interfaces and improved slot selection time sixfold through JVM and data-plane optimizations. Across the fleet, shuffle cost decreased by nearly 90% per task, while the proportion of executor runtime spent waiting on shuffle operations fell by approximately 10–15% from its peak.

Sources indicate that the converged Flink platform processes hundreds of millions of events per hour in historical backfills, completing multi-day workloads in single-digit hours. Thousands of pipelines now use unified Flink computations for nearline processing and historical corrections, replacing parallel Spark implementations. LinkedIn is exploring caching and faster upstream upgrades while continuing to contribute to Celeborn.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it’s been a… year, huh?
  • According to recent reports, technology hyperscalers like Microsoft and Meta, along with AI startups like Open AI and Anthropic have transformed everything about tech and the job we do.
  • It’s not just tech jobs that have transformed either.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it’s been a… year, huh? I think the most common emoji I’ve seen this year is 🫩 and that says a lot. One thing is for sure: the industry we make a living in is in flux, regardless of the outcomes of the AI bubble. Let’s take a look at how we can try and navigate that situation as best we can. But first….

According to recent reports, technology hyperscalers like Microsoft and Meta, along with AI startups like Open AI and Anthropic have transformed everything about tech and the job we do. This is true regardless of if they fail or somehow succeed in their quest to have everyone paying a subscription fee for their Large Language Model (LLM) technology, which is marketed to us as AI. I’ll refer to this technology as AI for the rest of this article for simplicity.

It’s not just tech jobs that have transformed either. Everywhere you go, you will see some slop, somewhere. Be it a flyer, website, a village poster or a food truck menu. Heck, people are even using LLMs to work out what’s special about their own children. The effects of this technology are far-reaching, way beyond our own industry.

According to recent reports, the technology has hit us all in tech especially hard though. Mid-last year, I did some investigating because I suspected that so-called AI mandates were becoming increasingly popular and what I learned from conversations then feels like some sort of utopia compared to now. In the space between that piece being published and now, we went from token maxxing to companies realizing that actually, this technology is extremely expensive and not returning the promised outcomes.

The mandates have cooled, sure, but the demands to use AI to produce more volume, regardless of whether that volume is actually needed or not are still very much there. I’m in a fortunate position to have friendships with people all across the industry, from tech hyperscalers, to tiny little studios, and the stories I have heard from their work life are nothing short of horrifying. No one really seems to be happy with their work either.

This is such a long way away from even a handful of years ago where yes, there was a lot of problematic culture and outcomes from the tech industry, but people were generally quite happy with the work they were doing at least.

The sudden urge to sprint towards AI technologies over the last few years has had a devastating effect in so many places. The technology has encouraged suicide, devastated communities with the data center build-out and of course, displaced thousands of people’s careers. It’s worth noting that I’ve mentioned only a tiny sample of the harms there. If I listed them all, this article would be unbearably long and depressing.

Sources indicate that some harms I do want to touch on though are the effects on our communities in tech. The community spirit of open source and open knowledge was the foundation of the industry’s — especially the web industry’s — rapid success. At the root of everything there was people happy to share knowledge and build everyone up with them. Those people still do exist — myself included — but being one of those people is increasingly difficult.

As the numbers go up in the AI world, the numbers very much go down for independent educators, publishers and community conferences. There’s a developing and worrying culture of “I don’t need to skill up now because I can use AI for work”, so allow me to break down why that reductive view of your work and your career is harmful in the long term.

Industry observers note that and don’t ever forget that! Let’s have a think for a second about what actually makes you a good developer, because typing characters in a text editor certainly isn’t it. What makes us good is experience, knowledge, nuance and above all else, creativity.

It has been revealed that look, I get it, AI really can feel like it’s a miracle machine, but it’s important to take a wider view. Along with the published studies on cognitive decline and the widening skills gap, it’s more important than ever to invest in your brain to keep your skills sharp because you’re not getting that repetitive reinforcement that writing code every day gives you anymore if AI tools do everything for you. There’s a reason that I often build most of my teaching around a linear build-along because the tangible nature of repeating patterns you’ve learned really helps that knowledge to sink in.

As always, this article is addressed to everyone, but I want to talk directly to founders (like me), decision makers, and managers for a second. A big part of our job, in fact, the most key part, is to ensure that our workers are looked after. I’m not just talking about compensation and perks here. I’m talking about our responsibility to ensure that our workers’ skills are kept sharp, their professional curiosities are satisfied and above all else that they are happy in the work they are doing. Our workers are much more than “number go up” vehicles.

You should be giving your developers more time to learn, rather than chasing endless volume. If AI enthusiasts are to be believed, there’s hours upon hours of time efficiencies created by this technology. Don’t fill that time with more volume. Instead, invest that time in developing your worker’s skills. It’s going to avoid burnout which yep, daily LLM use will likely cause in the long term.

One thing that is increasingly clear is that the health of the AI industry is not good. The bubble has already effectively burst in China and more worryingly for economy enjoyers, the “picks and shovels” — AKA the chips industry in Korea — has seen dramatic downturns. This is not how an “inevitable” outcome is supposed to happen!

The U.S. AI industry is on very shaky ground too. Circular financing, unbelievable levels of debt and a data center build out that simply cannot keep up with the required power levels to turn profits for hyperscalers and startups, mixed with a genuine hatred of the technology by the general public, creates enough risk in itself. Recent events, such as the Democrats dominating the midterms causing AI stocks to drop and as well as Nvidia’s stock because of its CEO being caught up in a spying scandal shine a light on the fragility of the industry. A healthy industry doesn’t work like this.

Industry observers note that with all that in mind, what would be a really silly thing to do? Yeh, you guessed it: put AI at the heart of everything in your business. Sure, there’s open source models — which I think is the logical destination of the technology — but how many companies are going to be willing to maintain their infrastructure needs? Not many. The low barrier of entry of commercial AI technology is the selling point, let’s be honest.

Above everything, people need to be invested in, not pushed aside by technology like AI. As I mentioned earlier, it’s experience, knowledge, nuance, and creativity that sets humans far apart from AI. That technology does indeed keep evolving, but even the most ardent of AI supporters will concede that the rate of frontier model improvement is very much levelling out.

There’s never been a more important time to keep human skills sharp, so here’s some ideas on how to do that.

This is not just directed at individuals but also at founders, decision makers and managers. Our industry has been historically excellent at investing in skilling people up and we need to bring that back.

Industry observers note that give staff the time and budget to learn, to develop their skills and to engage with the community at conferences. You already know the positive outcomes that brings, so bring it back to your organization. At the absolute worst case, it’ll make the usage of AI in your organization more efficient and when the token subsidies inevitably end, more cost effective.

Again, token subsidies will inevitably end. So, getting thousands of dollars of worth from a $200 a month subscription will be something you’ll look fondly back on. When hallucinations from AI tools are suddenly costing thousands, does it make sense to force your staff to produce as much volume as possible? Of course not.

It has been revealed that my advice is to re-evaluate those prior decisions and invest saved costs back into developing your workers instead, while there’s still a hope of them not burning out completely. Make sure you include your workers in these decisions and discuss the impacts of mandates on them. It’s important for you to understand the impact of these sort of decisions.

This advice is more aimed at developers, but stay paying attention, managers. As I noted earlier, repetition (especially typing) reinforces newly introduced learning and existing knowledge. The slower pace also allows your brain to think, which from a quality of output perspective, is imperative. Doing none of that atrophies skills over time.

According to recent reports, I recently read Jenn Schiffer’s great post. She did the Weird Web October challenge and wrote this:.

[…] i encourage anyone who uses ai and/or vibe codes to consider doing an exercise like this without those tools as a way to challenge your brain and you can continue doing your regular work the way you do your regular work.

I think that’s a very good idea, even if it’s messing around with a little side project — if you’ve got the energy from Producing Value all day, of course. Guess what bosses: this is another way you can make your staff happier, by giving them time to do this on the clock.

At the end of the day, you’ll miss the soul when it’s gone. It’s not gone yet though. Far from it. Independents like CSS-Tricks, my publication, Piccalilli, and Smashing Magazine are trying hard to keep the soul of our industry alive by sharing high quality educational content with the community.

Most of this content is free at the point of entry, but it certainly isn’t free to produce. We all pay writers fairly to share their knowledge with the community and we are all tiny organizations. We’re certainly not in this game to make huge profits, that’s for sure.

All of us could do more though, but funding is the ultimate barrier. For both companies and individuals, purchase courses, join the membership programs, and purchase ad space. With the right financial support, publications like ours can be a real force in pushing the good stuff back into our industry and bringing everyone up with us. That’s what we do it for.

Some course producers I recommend are Miriam, Sara, Mat, Scott, Brad and Ian, Josh, Ahmad, Christine, Vitaly, Ben and of course, myself! All of these will have generous Black Friday deals, so go ahead and ask your boss to invest in you.

Now, share this post with your boss.

8 Mac menu bar apps that actually earn their spot on a coding Mac (2026)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • You glance up at the menu bar to check something and it's a wall of 25 icons, half of which you can't name.
  • It has been revealed that the menu bar is the most valuable real estate on a Mac, and most of us let it fill up by accident.
  • An icon stays only if I look at it or click it at least once a day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know the moment. You glance up at the menu bar to check something and it's a wall of 25 icons, half of which you can't name. The MacBook notch has quietly eaten three of them.

It has been revealed that the menu bar is the most valuable real estate on a Mac, and most of us let it fill up by accident. Here's the short list of menu bar apps I'd actually let stay there on a Mac used for coding, and what each one earns its spot for.

An icon stays only if I look at it or click it at least once a day. Everything else gets hidden or quit. With that rule, these eight make the cut.

It has been revealed that ice is the first thing I'd install, because it fixes the problem every other item on this list creates. It hides and shows menu bar items so you keep only the ones you care about visible.

According to recent reports, it's free, open source, and needs macOS 14 or later. If you've ever lost an icon behind the notch, this is the fix.

Industry observers note that stats puts a system monitor in your menu bar: CPU, memory, disk, network, battery and more. You pick which modules show.

Handy when a build, a Docker container or a local model suddenly makes the fans spin up and you want to know why. Install with brew install stats or grab the DMG from the releases page.

Itsycal is a tiny menu bar calendar that reads from the Mac Calendar app. You can see and create events, view and complete Reminders, and join virtual meetings from it.

It has a configurable shortcut to open it, and yes, it supports Vim motions for navigation.

Sources indicate that maccy is a clipboard manager that does one job: keep your copy history and let you search it fast. Hit the shortcut, type, press Enter.

In a recent development, it's keyboard-first, stores everything on your Mac, and is MIT licensed. It needs macOS 14 or later. Once you have clipboard history you stop re-copying the same error message three times.

Amphetamine keeps your Mac awake with a simple switch in the menu bar, or automatically through Triggers.

You can keep it awake indefinitely, for a set time, while a file downloads, or while a specific app is running. Useful when a long test run or a coding agent is working and you step away.

CleanShot X is the screenshot and screen recording tool I'd pick for bug reports and PR descriptions. It adds annotation, a video editor with smart zooms, and optional cloud links.

Recent findings suggest that the Basic license is $35 once with a year of updates (optional renewal at $19 a year). Cloud Pro is $10 per user per month billed annually. It also comes with a Setapp subscription. It needs macOS 13 or later.

Recent findings suggest that rectangle moves and resizes windows with keyboard shortcuts or by dragging them to screen edges and corners. Repeat a shortcut to cycle through sizes.

Industry observers note that it lives in the menu bar for quick access to layouts. The free version is open source and supports macOS 14+. Rectangle Pro adds custom shortcuts for any size and position.

If you code with AI agents, the number you check most is probably how much of your limit is left and when it resets. TokenBar puts usage and reset times for Claude, Codex, Cursor, Gemini and Copilot in one menu bar view.

Recent findings suggest that it demonstrates things like session and weekly usage and a pace check against the reset. It's built on Peter Steinberger's MIT-licensed CodexBar and credits Pixel Agents for its agent status view. It doesn't give you any extra quota, it just shows you where you stand. Basic is $5/month, Pro is $15 lifetime, and it needs macOS 14 or later.

Recent findings suggest that weather, a second clock, VPN icons I only touch once a week, and every app that adds an icon by default and never asks. Those all go behind Ice.

What's the one menu bar app you'd never remove? Drop it in the comments, I'm always looking for a ninth.
