Jiff 1.0: A datetime library for Rust

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (5005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Burntsushi

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jiff is a datetime library for Rust that encourages you to jump into the pit of success.
  • Jiff is pronounced like “gif” with a soft “g,” as in “gem.”.
  • This blog announces the Jiff 1.0 release by giving a tour of its API.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jiff is a datetime library for Rust that encourages you to jump into the pit of success. Jiff automatically handles many common problems related to daylight saving time by putting time zone handling front and center into the API. Jiff has already seen widespread adoption in the Rust ecosystem.

Jiff is pronounced like “gif” with a soft “g,” as in “gem.”.

This blog announces the Jiff 1.0 release by giving a tour of its API.

Target audience: Rust programmers who need convenient datetime handling.

It has been revealed that jiff is already used in production in many projects: uv, Cargo, Starship, fd, Nushell, mise, Jujutsu, uutils/coreutils and even as the basis for a Temporal implementation in AWS LLRT. It is time to call it 1.0.

It has been revealed that unless some significant defect is found in Jiff’s API, my proposal is to commit to Jiff 1.0 indefinitely. This is crucial because the intent is for Jiff to be an ecosystem building block that appears in the public API of other libraries. This makes Jiff an attractive public dependency, which means semver incompatible releases are likely to cause significant pain in the ecosystem. They will not be made lightly.

To see a list of breaking changes between Jiff 0.2 and Jiff 1.0, please consult the CHANGELOG.

In programming, a datetime library’s core functionality rests at the intersection of a computer system’s concept of time and a human’s concept of time. The prevailing notion of system time is Unix time. A human’s concept of time is far more complex, but the most popular such model is the Gregorian calendar coupled with either a 12-hour or 24-hour clock. At the core of every datetime library rests some routine for converting between these concepts.

Sources indicate that A datetime library typically provides much more than this. Indeed, datetime handling has historically been very difficult. My own belief is that the difficulty comes from poor modeling of the domain. Instead of encapsulating the complexity inside a reusable bundle of code, many datetime libraries pass some or all of the complexity on to its people. Jiff instead tries hard to encapsulate the complexity and make it difficult for users to do something wrong. (Jiff is not the first to do this!).

In this section of the blog, we’ll do some very basic introductions.

To follow along with the examples in this blog, create a new Cargo project with dependencies on jiff and anyhow:.

Most examples are a complete self-contained Rust program. Just copy the code and replace whatever is in src/main.rs. Then run the program:.

I am loath to present a dictionary. However, the datetime domain is littered with confusable terms, so I think it’s important to orient ourselves on a shared vocabulary. I’ve kept this section as small as possible. (Some terms, like “time zone,” are omitted here because they are best defined through exploration in the sections that follow.).

TAI and leap seconds won’t be a feature of this blog, but they are listed here in order to convey the difference between Unix time and UTC.

In a recent development, as a way to transition into some of the core types of Jiff, I’ve come to think of its datetime types like an onion. In reverse order, we can build up its layers all the way to a ZonedDateTime. So let’s start with more terms, but this time, they are also types in Jiff:.

According to recent reports, to make this a bit more concrete, we can see what this looks like in code. Since a time zone can map from a civil datetime to an instant in time, one way to create a zoned datetime requires only a civil datetime and a time zone:.

Sources indicate that another way to create a zoned datetime requires only a timestamp and a time zone. This is because time zones can also map a timestamp to a particular civil datetime:.

According to recent reports, notice how we get the equivalent zoned datetime in both cases, but we come at it from different directions. In the first case, we start with a time that we might see on our clocks and calendars. In the second case, we start with a particular instant in time that we might get from a database or file system or some other system call.

In a recent development, there is one piece missing from the zoned datetime onion examples: the time zone offset. An offset represents the amount of time one must adjust UTC time in order to get civil time. For example, consider the time 2026-11-01T22:30:00 in UTC. In order to get the civil datetime for someone living in New York, one would subtract 5 hours:.

Indeed, every zoned datetime has an offset associated with it:.

Industry observers note that NOTE: The America/New_York string you see in the above example is an IANA Time Zone Database Identifier. The IANA Time Zone Database is a collection of time zone definitions that can be referenced by a short identifier string. Examples: Australia/Sydney, Asia/Tokyo, Europe/Berlin.

When a civil datetime is combined with an offset, then what you get is always an instant in time.

Sources indicate that with the concept of an offset introduced, we can now give a more precise definition of a time zone. A time zone is a geographic region in which civil clocks agree and which provides the following:.

In a recent development, both mappings have been demonstrated in prior examples, but the mapping from civil datetime to an offset seems to be rather complicated due to some potential ambiguity. When does that ambiguity arise? An ambiguous offset occurs when the civil datetime either doesn’t correspond to a valid clock time in this time zone (e.g., when clocks are moved ahead for daylight saving time) or where there could be multiple valid clock times (e.g., when clocks are moved backward for daylight saving time).

Recent findings suggest that let’s look at some examples. In this first example, we’ll take a look at times around the daylight saving time transition from summer time to standard time in Upcoming York. In New York, the clocks were “set back” by an hour at exactly 2AM. This caused the 1AM hour to repeat itself.

It has been revealed that the above example shows how Jiff resolves the ambiguity when a “fold” occurs, or when there is a time zone transition that moves the civil time backwards. But we can actually dig down into lower level APIs to change how that ambiguity is resolved. By default, Jiff uses a “compatible” strategy that always selects the first repetition of a time in a fold. But other strategies can be selected by using APIs on a TimeZone directly:.

Sources indicate that the same idea applies to gaps, or time zone transitions where there’s some civil time that gets skipped on civil clocks. For example, on March 8, 2026 at 2AM, civil time skipped ahead to 3AM:.

There are two remaining core types, both representing some notion of a duration:.

A Span is the preferred duration type to use whenever possible. Here’s a simple example that reveals how to get the number of days between two civil dates:.

Durations can also be added to dates:.

Generally speaking, whenever there is an operation involving a Span, there is an equivalent operation available with SignedDuration:.

According to recent reports, notice that in the above example, we actually switched from using a civil::Date to a civil::DateTime. This was done to show how physical time units can be added. But note that the same can be accomplished with a Span, because it combines all units:.

Industry observers note that in brief, use a Span when you can. But when it’s too bulky or too slow, use a SignedDuration. One of the key benefits of a Span is that since it represents each unit value distinctly, one can preserve the original meaning of a duration. For example, it’s common to represent the runtime of films in minutes, even when the duration exceeds one hour. Indeed, a span of 2 hours is a distinct span from a span of 120 minutes:.

Industry observers note that the Span::fieldwise routine converts a Span into a value whose units can be compared in a field-by-field fashion. To compare spans based on the actual physical duration they represent, use Span::compare:.

Sources indicate that this was a very brief introduction to durations in Jiff. They are a lot more powerful than what is shown here. You might even try playing with the examples above to explore its nooks and crannies. We’ll cover their API in more detail in a later section.

Recent findings suggest that jiff isn’t always the right thing to use. Sometimes you can get by with something simpler.

First and foremost, if you’re measuring the time something takes in a program, you should almost certainly be using monotonic time. This is available via std::time::Instant:.

If you do need to compute elapsed time using your system clock, then Jiff is very convenient for that:.

But you don’t actually need Jiff for this. A std::time::SystemTime will work perfectly fine:.

Where Jiff starts to become useful is when you need something beyond just an integer number of seconds since the Unix epoch. For example, some very hairy math is required in order to convert a SystemTime into an RFC 3339 timestamp like 2026-11-14T21:34:00Z.

As long as you can live in UTC completely, don’t care about local time and can work with Unix timestamps only, then the Rust standard library won’t steer you wrong.

In a recent development, conversion to and from strings is a major part of Jiff. Jiff’s focus is primarily on interoperability via the following:.

What Jiff actually implements is the Temporal RFC 9557 / ISO 8601 grammar for flexible parsing of datetimes from strings. For most use cases, it suffices to think in terms of RFC 3339, RFC 9557 or ISO 8601. But Jiff does support parsing strings that aren’t valid in any of those three specifications. For example, 2026-11-12[America/New_York] parses as if it was 2026-11-12T00:00:00[America/New_York].

In this section, we’ll take a tour of how Jiff does datetime formatting and printing.

Every datetime and duration type in Jiff implements the standard library FromStr and Display traits. This means that it’s natural to parse datetimes:.

Parsing is flexible, so even if there are components missing, parsing still succeeds. For example, without minutes or seconds, those components default to zero:.

In a recent development, another example of flexible parsing is that if a string contains another date type, then one can parse that. For example, one can parse a date out of an ISO 8601 datetime:.

A ZonedDateTime always uses RFC 9557 syntax, which includes the IANA time zone identifier:.

If you want to print a zoned datetime using only RFC 3339 syntax, then you can do so by formatting the timestamp directly with the zoned datetime’s offset:.

Industry observers note that the Span and SignedDuration types also support the FromStr and Display traits via the ISO 8601 duration format. For example:.

Industry observers note that since a Span is a hybrid duration that also supports calendar units, it can parse durations with calendar units and physical time units. A SignedDuration can only parse durations with physical time units:.

The ISO 8601 duration format does, however, have some shortcomings that we’ll discuss in the next section.

Because ISO 8601 duration strings enjoy broad support, it is the default in Jiff for both Span and SignedDuration. However, it has two key shortcomings:.

Industry observers note that the second shortcoming is best seen with an example. Consider a Span that is 2000 milliseconds. If you convert this to an ISO 8601 duration string and then parse it back, you end up with 2 seconds instead:.

This might not be desirable for cases where you want a span’s string format to faithfully represent all possible distinct values of a span.

For these two reasons, Jiff comes with its own bespoke “friendly” duration format. The friendly format is non-lossy and is meant to be easier to read for English speakers than the ISO 8601 duration format. Here are some examples that are all valid friendly durations:.

Parsing a friendly duration is as easy as parsing an ISO 8601 duration: the FromStr implementations on both Span and SignedDuration support ISO 8601 durations and friendly durations simultaneously:.

In a recent development, printing a friendly duration does require a bit more effort, since it isn’t the default. Instead of Span::to_string(), one can use the “alternative” syntax via Rust’s formatting machinery:.

In a recent development, one can also use a lower level friendly printer to customize its output. For example, here’s how to write a span in the friendly format to an existing String using more spacing, longer unit labels and commas separating each unit:.

See the jiff::fmt::friendly module for a lot more detail, including a grammar that precisely specifies the format supported.

The POSIX strptime and POSIX strftime routines are far from the ideal way to format and parse datetimes, but they are ubiquitous and most programmers are familiar with them. Because of their ubiquity, and because of the utility of being able to format and parse bespoke datetime formats, Jiff provides implementations of these routines that are mostly POSIX compatible.

Recent findings suggest that every datetime type in Jiff comes with strptime and strftime routines. For example, to parse a civil date in the US month/day/year format:.

Or to format a zoned datetime in a convenient to read representation for English speakers:.

Callers can also use lower level APIs from jiff::fmt::strtime to get access to each parsed component individually:.

While the above tour should cover most use cases, there are sometimes reasons for exerting more control over parsing or formatting. Or for supporting alternate formats like RFC 2822. The jiff::fmt module is meant to cover these use cases at the cost of more complex APIs. For example, consider parsing an RFC 2822 datetime string from a &[u8] (which lets callers avoid a UTF-8 validation check):.

Another example indicates how to change the default disambiguation strategy when the provided civil datetime is ambiguous. For example, Sydney, Australia moved the clocks backwards at 2026-04-05T03:00:00 local time. That is, they went from UTC offset +11 to UTC offset +10. So what happens if we try to parse a time on the clock that is repeated as a result?

It has been revealed that here, the first occurrence of 02:30 is selected, just before Sydney leaves daylight saving time. Now, the data itself can actually select the desired offset:.

Sources indicate that but this happens because there is no ambiguity in the data. Since the offset is supplied, the exact instant in time is known. Going back to 2026-04-05T02:30[Australia/Sydney], which is ambiguous because it could refer to two different instants in time, how do we modify the strategy for resolving that ambiguity? We can’t using the standard library FromStr trait, so we instead have to construct our own parser manually, just like we did for RFC 2822 parsing above. This example shows how to do that and all of the different disambiguation options. Remember, UTC offset +11:00 corresponds to the first occurrence of 2026-04-05T02:30 on the clocks of folks in Sydney while UTC offset +10:00 corresponds to the second occurrence.

The jiff::fmt module contains lots of other goodies that we won’t cover here, including, but not limited to:.

Industry observers note that no section on datetime formatting would be complete without addressing locales. In this context, a locale is a set of user preferences used for formatting datetimes. This is useful when you want to present a datetime to an end user that doesn’t expect standard formats from RFC 3339, RFC 9557 or ISO 8601.

Industry observers note that jiff itself does not provide any facilities for dealing with locales. Instead, consumers can opt into this support via the ICU4X project. To make conversions between Jiff and ICU4X, the jiff-icu integration crate can be used.

Here’s an example showing how to format a zoned datetime in the fr-LA locale: (You’ll need to run cargo add icu jiff-icu to your project for this to work.).

Industry observers note that the ICU4X API has a lot of options for customizing datetime formatting. Exploring it further is outside the scope of this blog.

Jiff provides many methods on its datetime types to make using them as comfortable and error-free as possible.

Industry observers note that every datetime type provides a newly introduced constructor that lets callers build it from its constituent parts. In most cases, this constructor is fallible. For example:.

Because creating dates is so common, there is a shorthand for doing so when you know the inputs are valid:.

Industry observers note that that is, civil::date is a const function that will panic if its inputs are invalid. It should only be used with inputs that are known to be valid. It would, for example, be inappropriate to use this with user provided values. Because of the const block above, if you try to provide invalid values, you’ll get a compiler error.

For datetime types that represent an instant in time (i.e., ZonedDateTime and Timestamp), there is also a now() constructor for getting the current time:.

In addition to constructors, newly introduced date values can be constructed from old date values using the Date::with API:.

Once you have a date, there are oodles of APIs available:.

Moreover, because of the datetime onion, all of these APIs are also available on civil::DateTime and ZonedDateTime:.

These routines on ZonedDateTime also take time zone transitions into account. For example, ZonedDateTime knows that tomorrow() doesn’t always add 24 hours:.

NOTE: We’ll talk about date arithmetic in the next section.

When ZonedDateTime::tomorrow() (among other APIs that produce a ZonedDateTime) would land in a gap or a fold, the “compatible” disambiguation strategy is chosen automatically:.

To override this behavior, you can drop down to civil datetimes, perform the operation, and then use TimeZone::to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime to control the exact disambiguation strategy:.

According to recent reports, there are a few other methods of note on date types that are worth mentioning. First is the ability to query for things like, “The Thursday after next” or “The last Sunday of the month.” The former can be answered by the nth_weekday API:.

While the latter can be answered by the nth_weekday_of_month API:.

Finally, customers can access a convenient time series iterator via series:.

All of these methods are also available on civil::Date and civil::DateTime, which should make it very natural to move between them.

According to recent reports, all datetime types in Jiff support adding and subtracting durations, and finding the span of time between two datetime values. Let’s start with a civil::Date:.

Here we make use of the std::ops::Add trait implementation for civil::Date. The downside of using this, though, is that if the date value goes out of range, then it panics. That may or may not be acceptable. But if you’re dealing with user inputs, then you should use Date::checked_add instead:.

Let’s take a look at a few other examples involving months and years:.

As with other methods on Date, they are also available on ZonedDateTime:.

If we take a look at the type signature for ZonedDateTime::checked_add, we can see that it’s actually polymorphic:.

Industry observers note that specifically, it accepts anything that can be converted into a ZonedDateTimeArithmetic. In this case, there are From trait implementations for the following types:.

This means that ZonedDateTime::checked_add can accept any one of these duration values:.

Sources indicate that this type of polymorphism is common in Jiff. Here, it is merely used to provide a convenient way to use multiple duration types. But as we’ll see, it’s also used to provide an extension point for configuration options that control how the operation works.

In addition to adding or subtracting durations from datetime values, one can also compute the duration between two datetime values. For example, to get the number of days between two dates:.

Similarly, we can use Date::until to compute the span between dates:.

Like with Date::checked_add, this routine is also available at ZonedDateTime::until:.

Notice though that hours, instead of days, are returned. This is because two ZonedDateTime values might be in different time zones. Since a ZonedDateTime is fundamentally an instant in time, and because days might be of varying length depending on the time zone, defaulting to hours as the largest possible unit means subtracting two zoned datetimes will always succeed. However, we can request larger units in the duration returned by passing additional options. Notably, ZonedDateTime::until is polymorphic:.

That is, callers aren’t just limited to passing a ZonedDateTime here, but anything that can be converted to a ZonedDateTimeDifference. Here is one such example, where we can override the largest units returned in the duration:.

In a recent development, A ZonedDateTimeDifference provides much more powerful configuration options for rounding the span returned. Take this example, which produces a span with many unit values:.

Recent findings suggest that this might be too much precision to show to an end user. Instead, perhaps we’d like to round the span to the nearest half-hour. We can do this by building a ZonedDateTimeDifference explicitly and configuring its options:.

Sources indicate that note also that rounding a span takes time zone transitions like daylight saving time into account. For example, let’s take 2024-11-02 17:30 and 2024-11-03 04:45 in New York. Because New York stopped daylight saving time at 2AM on 2024-11-03, the amount of physical time between them is 12 hours and 15 minutes:.

Normally, if we rounded to the nearest day, this would round up to 1 day. But since the midpoint of this particular day is actually 12 hours and 30 minutes, this duration will round down to 0 days when we request it:.

Next we’ll continue our discussion of rounding, but when applied to datetimes themselves.

Date rounding in Jiff is limited to units of days or lower. Therefore, it’s only available on ZonedDateTime, Timestamp, civil::DateTime, civil::Time but not civil::Date.

Industry observers note that A common example for rounding a datetime is to reduce precision. For example, a system clock might provide nanosecond precision, but maybe we only care about the nearest half-hour:.

As with rounding spans, rounding a ZonedDateTime is aware of time zone transitions:.

It has been revealed that notice that in the above example, our time of 11:45AM is before noon, yet the result still rounds up to the next day. This is because the midpoint for this day is 11:30AM since, by 11:30AM, 12.5 hours have already elapsed because of the repeated 1AM hour in the move away from daylight saving time in New York.

Sources indicate that jiff itself doesn’t support any calendars other than the proleptic Gregorian calendar. One can instead use the ICU4X crate to work in non-Gregorian calendars, and convert between datetime types using the jiff-icu crate: (Use cargo add icu jiff-icu to make this example work.).

The ICU4X API supports many more calendars.

There are 3 potentially confusable datetime types in Jiff:.

When should you use each one versus the other?

Sources indicate that to a first approximation, if you can use a ZonedDateTime, then that is probably the type you want to reach for. It represents a specific instant in time in a particular geographic location. That is, it has both a Timestamp and a TimeZone.

It has been revealed that if you only ever need to work in UTC or just deal with system time, then a Timestamp is probably the right choice. This is useful for representing a specific instant in time that is not connected to any time zone.

A civil::DateTime is useful in contexts where you don’t care about a specific instant in time and when calcuations should be done independent of time zone. For example, when parsing datetime information from a user interface datetime picker.

Remember that both a civil::DateTime and a Timestamp can be converted to a ZonedDateTime by supplying a time zone.

Sources indicate that we’ve already seen how to add spans to datetime values and how to get spans as a difference between datetime values. But we haven’t yet explored the APIs available on a Span itself.

First and foremost, we can build a Span through its constructor, which returns a Span with all of its units set to 0:.

A Span is both Copy and immutable. We can create newly introduced spans through method chaining:.

Or we can use the ToSpan convenience trait, which adds methods on integer types for constructing spans:.

It has been revealed that note though that methods like Span::hours and ToSpan::hours will panic when the integer is outside the limits of what Span supports. This is fine when your spans are literals in your program, since a panic would indicate a bug. But if your inputs come from an end user, it’s better to use fallible methods:.

Spans preserve each individual unit value. This means that 90 minutes and 1 hour 30 minutes, while they represent the same duration, are actually different values in memory:.

According to recent reports, this permits callers maximum flexibility when it comes to representing durations. This makes it possible to represent durations in a specific unit even when they add up to larger units. For example, the runtime duration of films is typically conveyed in minutes, even when the runtime exceeds one hour. This can be adjusted programmatically using Span::round:.

You can go the other way as well:.

Industry observers note that neither of these examples do actual rounding, despite the name of the API. Instead, since we’re only setting the largest unit, this API is doing unit balancing. Unit balancing is when all unit values rollover into larger units up until the largest configured unit. This works even for calendar units too, but you need to provide a relative date:.

It has been revealed that without a relative date, it’s not possible to know how many hours are in a single month. That is, once calendar units are involved, a span cannot be interpreted as a physical duration of time until some context is applied.

It has been revealed that the same even applies to days themselves, since days can sometimes be more or less than 24 hours. Take the above example. What happens if we use a zoned datetime as our relative date instead?

Notice that the duration’s hour component changed from 20 to 21. Why? Because we started with 2756 hour in both cases and because 2020-03-29 in Rome was only 23 hours long (in a move from standard time to daylight saving time). That means that one of those days in 3mo 23d was only 23 hours long. So an extra hour needed to be added to make up for it.

The round API can also do actual rounding:.

You can also change its rounding mode from the default (“half-expand”, or like you were taught rounding in school) to truncation (or one of several other modes):.

According to recent reports, one can also specify a rounding increment to round to the nearest unit value. For example, to the nearest half-hour:.

Because a Span value cannot easily be compared correctly based purely on its value in memory, a dedicated comparison Span::compare routine is provided:.

According to recent reports, also, one can convert a Span to a floating point value in terms of any unit. For example:.

Converting to calendar units requires a relative date for the same reasons discussed above:.

It has been revealed that so far, we’ve explored a good chunk of Jiff’s API. We didn’t talk about every nook and cranny, but I think we’ve covered the most important pieces.

We’ll wrap up by briefly discussing motivation and inspiration.

Whenever I needed datetime handling in Rust, I always got confused. Should I use chrono or time? How do I get my local time from a timestamp? How do I use my system’s time zone database? How do I do calendar arithmetic?

Recent findings suggest that before I started working on Jiff, this confusion got annoying enough for me to consider writing my own crate. I felt like the APIs of both chrono and time could be improved upon. I personally found the domain quite interesting and so set out to build something better.

It has been revealed that why not improve on an existing solution, like chrono or time, instead of adding yet another choice into the ecosystem? I do think there are material downsides of having too many choices, but I had concluded that both chrono and time (in 2024) had reached a local maximum. Moreover, in 2024, I was not an expert in datetime handling. It took building a datetime library to become one. So convincing crate maintainers to go in a radically different direction would have been a tall order.

Jiff’s design and comparison documentation contain much more detail regarding the motivation and specific examples between Jiff, chrono and time.

Jiff is heavily inspired by Temporal, which is JavaScript’s standard library solution for date and time management. Jiff inherits API design, functionality and even parsing/formatting of datetime values. Note though that Jiff is not and does not aim to be a 100% compatible implementation of the Temporal specification. Jiff is meant to be a Rust ecosystem library first and foremost.

It has been revealed that with that said, if you’re familiar with Temporal and Rust, then it’s likely you’ll find Jiff to be a relatively straightforward translation of Temporal’s API to Rust. This example shows how to use Temporal to round a calendar span to the nearest number of days relative to a date:.

And here’s the equivalent operation in Jiff:.

Industry observers note that the main difference between these examples is that Jiff’s duration type is named Span instead of Duration. This was done to avoid confusion with Rust’s standard library std::time::Duration type.

Here are some other differences:.

It’s easy to say that without Temporal, Jiff wouldn’t exist in its current form today.

#329. Grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays

Grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1062 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cornell

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that two latest research papers shed light on the growing practice of grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays.
  • According to recent reports, A team from the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS) found that when two sheep per hectare graze around solar arrays, the abundance of wild bees, honey bees and lady beetles jumped by 38%, compared to a control plot that was mowed.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Sheep grazing and beneficial insect habitat are two prominent conversation topics around solar development right now,” stated Leana Zoller, the paper’s first author and a postdoctoral associate in natural resources in the Cornell CALS Ashley School of Global Development and the Environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A solar farm in Lansing, Upcoming York.

Industry observers note that two latest research papers shed light on the growing practice of grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays. One demonstrates that, in the right numbers, sheep grazing increases populations of beneficial insects like bees and lady beetles compared to mowing around solar panels. The other research describes a decision-making support tool to help farmers profitably grow their solar grazing herds.

According to recent reports, A team from the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS) found that when two sheep per hectare graze around solar arrays, the abundance of wild bees, honey bees and lady beetles jumped by 38%, compared to a control plot that was mowed. The increase was driven primarily by an 83% increase in honey bees alone, according to the team’s findings in “Low solar-grazing densities support beneficial insects in agrivoltaic systems,” published Oct. 7 in Environmental Research Letters.

Recent findings suggest that “Sheep grazing and beneficial insect habitat are two prominent conversation topics around solar development right now,” stated Leana Zoller, the paper’s first author and a postdoctoral associate in natural resources in the Cornell CALS Ashley School of Global Development and the Environment. “But what’s been missing is research that treats them as parts of the same system. When we talk about sustainable solar development, integrating these discussions into a single framework is really helpful to farmers and community decision makers.”.

For three years, Zoller and a team of entomologists, ecologists and animal and plant scientists tested various stocking rates – how many sheep per hectare are allowed to graze a certain plot of land – using Cornell’s teaching sheep grazing at the university-owned Cascadilla Community Solar Farm in Dryden, Fresh York. At four sheep per hectare, they found beneficial insect abundance was similar to the mowed control site, while vegetation management effectiveness was greater than at two sheep per hectare. At eight sheep per hectare, vegetation management was maximized and sheep flock health remained high, but honey bee abundance dropped by 45%.

“We zeroed in on stocking rates because that’s a concrete number that sheep farmers understand and work with every day, and we want this research to be useful,” noted Steve Grodsky, paper senior author and assistant professor of natural resources in the Ashley School. “With solar grazing, people, energy, agricultural animals, plants and insects are all part of this ecosystem. We’re trying to understand the connections between those pieces so that when solar developers, municipalities looking at solar development, or farmers are faced with a decision, they can have scientific information about potential trade-offs and synergies.”.

Grodsky is also assistant unit leader of the U.S. Geological Survey New York Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit. Additional co-authors are sheep farmer and solar grazing consultant Nikola Kochendoerfer, Ph.D. ’20; Antonio DiTommaso, professor in the School of Integrative Plant Science; John Losey, professor of entomology; Scott McArt, Ph.D. ’12, associate professor of entomology; Paige Muñiz, formerly a technician in McArt’s lab; and Todd Ugine, Ph.D. ’04, research associate in Losey’s lab, all in CALS. Sarah Carson, director of Cornell’s Campus Sustainability Office, was key in coordinating site access between researchers and the solar company that manages the Cascadilla solar farm.

Recent findings suggest that another Cornell research team, from the Cornell SC Johnson College of Business, has developed a tool that helps farmers whose sheep graze in solar arrays to make better decisions about their operation. The team described the tool in “Flock Management for Solar Grazing,” which published Sept. 28 in Manufacturing & Service Operations Management.

According to recent reports, after a chance encounter with Caleb Scott, Ithaca-based sheep farmer and founder of United Agrivoltaics, Vincent Slaugh, assistant professor at the Cornell Peter and Stephanie Nolan School of Hotel Administration and first author of the paper, began thinking through the economics and logistics of solar grazing. He recruited Linwei Xin, associate professor of operations research and information engineering, and Shane Henderson, Charles W. Lake, Jr. Professor in Productivity, both in the Cornell Duffield College of Engineering, to work on the topic.

In a recent development, together, they developed a spreadsheet-based model that helps sheep farmers to optimize procurement and sales decisions, based on factors like target flock size, costs, anticipated revenues, and expected vegetation in particular solar sites; if a farmer doesn’t have enough sheep to keep the grass down, they’ll have to cut it some other way. It also helps solar developers understand growers’ needs and develop contracts that are more profitable and sustainable for all parties long-term. United Agrivoltaics has already incorporated the tool into its onboarding process.

Slaugh sees opportunity for U.S. shepherds to grow their operations – especially with solar contracts offering a steady source of income and animal feed. Current domestic sheep production for meat and wool doesn’t come close to meeting domestic demand; about half of all lamb and mutton consumed in the U.S. is imported, primarily from Latest Zealand and Australia.

Industry observers note that “If we grow the sheep industry, will the American diet eventually include more lamb? Could that be a side effect of the solar energy revolution? I think the answer is very likely yes,” Slaugh said. “And then when that happens, we’d expect processors and supporting industries to come back, for banks to be willing to give more loans, and for supply chains to follow. All of that grows the economy, and rural economies in particular.”.

Kochendoerfer, who grazes 700 ewes on solar installations in Latest York and Vermont, said that economy is already growing.

Sources indicate that “I work with a lot of farms that are now scaling up because of solar,” Kochendoerfer remarked. “There is a newly introduced wave of sheep farmers who are capitalizing on this access to good land. With solar grazing, you get paid to graze as opposed to having to pay to graze. That leads to sustainable, meaningful economic income that these farmers can use to expand, build a barn, buy equipment or hire someone. It’s enabling a lot of folks to build sound, viable agricultural businesses.”.

Funding for these research projects came from the Cornell Atkinson Center for Sustainability, the National Institute for Food and Agriculture and the National Science Foundation.

Krisy Gashler is a writer for the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We’re excited to announce Aristotle’s expansion into Rust, one of the fastest-growing programming languages for high-stakes software.

The expansion builds on Aristotle’s support of C and Verilog and marks a major advancement in our mission to verify all code. Instead of relying on testing to catch every flaw, developers can now use Aristotle to prove their Rust code works as intended before it ships, providing a fresh level of certainty to systems where even a single bug can be catastrophic.

Industry observers note that with support for Rust, Aristotle can prove that your code has no undefined behavior and does exactly what its spec states, even inside unsafe blocks. If you’re rewriting C in Rust, it can prove the new code behaves the same as the original.

According to recent reports, “Rust is where much of the world’s most critical upcoming code is being written, and increasingly, AI is the one writing it,” remarked our CEO Tudor Achim. “With Aristotle, organizations can now prove their code does exactly what it’s supposed to, from the smart contracts that move money to the infrastructure that keeps systems running.”.

Sources indicate that rust powers software across mission-critical industries, from cloud computing and cybersecurity to automotive, aerospace, and financial services including crypto. It’s the backbone of Solana’s smart contracts that drive trading, lending, payments, and other DeFi services on the Solana blockchain.

According to recent reports, these systems have no room for error. Smart-contract transactions can’t be undone, so a single missed bug is all attackers need to drain hundreds of millions of dollars. Instead of relying on slow, manual audits that are outdated immediately after they’re published, Aristotle runs on every new line of code, proving it behaves as intended across all possible inputs and catching critical flaws before code goes live.

You can see it on real Solana programs. On Manifest, an open-source order book, Aristotle proved 28 results across the whole order book, including that a valid swap goes through, and found a rounding bug the team has since fixed. At Project 0, a prime broker, it proved the books stay consistent through deposits, withdrawals, borrows, repayments, and liquidations, in any order.

To bring that protection to more developers, we’re partnering with the Solana Foundation to support established Solana programs and help latest builders verify their smart contracts.

Industry observers note that “When software moves real money, security has to keep pace with every code change,” noted Ludo Galabru at the Solana Foundation. “Aristotle makes formal verification more accessible to Solana developers, helping teams check critical properties of their programs before launch and keep verifying them with every patch.”.

According to recent reports, aristotle for Rust is available today. Get started at aristotle.harmonic.fun with self-serve, consumption-based pricing, or contact bd@harmonic.fun for volume pricing, dedicated support, and custom deployment.

Press inquiries: pr@harmonic.fun.

#327. Latest Update: Michael Mann's 'Heat' Copyright Fight Turns on a Deal with Himself

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1996 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Copyrightlately

Latest Update: Michael Mann's 'Heat' Copyright Fight Turns on a Deal with Himself

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1996 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Copyrightlately

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New Regency indicates the director can’t reclaim rights in “Heat” because he wrote it for his own tech giant.
  • The most famous scene in Michael Mann’s Heat is a six-minute cup of coffee.
  • In a recent development, A lawsuit filed Friday in Los Angeles federal court describes a similar meeting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New Regency indicates the director can’t reclaim rights in “Heat” because he wrote it for his own tech giant. Mann says he wrote the early drafts on his own, not as his loan-out’s employee.

The most famous scene in Michael Mann’s Heat is a six-minute cup of coffee. Al Pacino’s cop and Robert De Niro’s thief, sharing the screen for the first time, sit across a table and discover they’re more or less the same guy.

In a recent development, A lawsuit filed Friday in Los Angeles federal court describes a similar meeting. According to New Regency’s complaint, Mann is trying to reclaim rights in his early Heat screenplay drafts based on a 1988 deal in which Michael Mann met with Michael Mann and assigned those drafts to two companies he controlled. Nobody wrote anything down. The studio claims Mann only recently “discovered” the alleged oral agreement with himself “after forgetting about it for nearly four decades,” and that when it asked for proof, his story changed.

But first, to see why this lawsuit landed now, we need a bit of the Heat 2 backstory.

Industry observers note that mann published Heat 2, a novel he co-wrote with Meg Gardiner, in 2022. According to the complaint, New Regency then licensed the sequel film rights to one of Mann’s companies. Warner Bros. came aboard in 2023 to co-produce, and Mann delivered a script in March 2025. Warner Bros. reportedly balked at Mann’s $170 million budget and let him shop the project elsewhere. In October 2025, the trades unveiled that Amazon MGM’s United Artists was picking up the project, with Leonardo DiCaprio and Christian Bale set to star. Asked about the move at a festival in Lyon, Mann told reporters, “I can’t get into all the politics of it.”.

Industry observers note that the complaint gets into some of those politics. Upcoming Regency claims Warner’s license reverted to it when the studio passed. Then, on April 29, 2026, months before the Amazon agreements described in the complaint were signed, Mann served New Regency with a notice purporting to terminate its rights in Heat. Two more termination notices followed in May.

Amazon’s apparent response was to buy the sequel rights twice. According to the complaint, Mann granted Amazon in October whatever Heat 2 rights he “may personally recapture” under his termination notices, and a few days later, Fresh Regency granted Amazon “certain of” its own rights. Both agreements acknowledge the dispute, and some of each side’s promises about title to the Heat screenplay depend on how it comes out. It’s like buying insurance from two companies, each of which insists the other’s policy is worthless.

New Regency sued on November 13. Mann’s spokesperson told Variety the case is “unrelated to production of Heat 2,” which is scheduled to start shooting January 19. With agreements from both sides, Amazon may be covered for the sequel either way, though the complaint states nothing about what comes after it.

A quick refresher for anyone who skipped my last few articles on this (it’s fine, they were long).

Sources indicate that now add the loan-out organization. Hollywood writers and directors commonly work through corporations they own, which formally employ them and lend their services to studios (hence the name). If you write a screenplay as an employee of your own company, the company is the legal author. It can’t terminate, because it’s a company. You can’t terminate, because you’re not the author. And even when the artist is the author, courts haven’t let artists terminate deals their loan-outs signed. As the judge in John Waite’s case put it, “people cannot use a corporate structure for some purposes—e.g. taking advantage of tax benefits—and then disavow it for others.”.

So Mann needs three things: a piece of Heat he wrote as himself, a grant of that piece that he made personally, and a link between that grant and the rights Latest Regency actually holds. New Regency says he has none of them.

According to recent reports, heat took almost twenty years to reach the screen, and Newly introduced Regency notes Mann called his writing a work for hire at every step. The complaint lays out the paper trail. In 1976, his new loan-out, the Michael Mann Manufacturer, lent his services to Columbia Pictures for a TV crime project. In 1989, the paperwork for an NBC movie called L.A. Takedown recited that he wrote the teleplay as “an employee-for-hire” of the loan-out and “reserved no rights.” And in 1994, the loan-out sold Warner Bros. the Heat screenplay as material Mann wrote “as a work made for hire.” Mann signed for the company and again for himself.

Recent findings suggest that but none of those agreements dates from 1981 to 1985, and that’s the period Mann is focusing on. According to the complaint, Mann now says he wrote early Heat drafts in those years on his own, as what Upcoming Regency calls “an unemployed author.” (That window covers Thief, The Keep and the launch of Miami Vice, so as unemployment goes, it was a pretty productive stretch.) Mann’s spokesperson told Variety the dispute concerns “original and personal writing Michael Mann did on multiple screenplays during the 1980s.”.

That’s different from the argument made by Road House writer Lance Hill, who calls his loan-out an “alter ego” that should be disregarded for purposes of termination. Mann, as Fresh Regency tells it, accepts that his loan-out was real. He just says he wasn’t working for it at the time he wrote the good stuff.

Industry observers note that next Mann needs a personal grant. His first termination notice identified an October 1, 1988 agreement with two companies he controlled: his loan-out and ZZY, Inc. Upcoming Regency says that when it asked for a copy, Mann’s lawyer explained there wasn’t one, because the agreement was oral. When the studio pressed for evidence, it says, the loan-out dropped out of the deal. A second notice followed, this time identifying an agreement between Mann and ZZY alone. New Regency likens Mann to “a Shakespearean actor playing multiple parts.”.

According to recent reports, the third termination notice concerns a written 1989 agreement assigning L.A. Takedown material to another Mann firm, Ajar, Inc. The complaint states the rights Mann assigned personally came from an earlier Columbia project, which was never produced and which he may have reacquired under a Writers Guild agreement. Upcoming Regency replies that reacquiring rights doesn’t change authorship: if the 1976 project was Columbia’s work for hire, it still is.

Recent findings suggest that so altogether, Mann has served three termination notices aimed at two different grants. Nearly all of this is Upcoming Regency’s version of events. Mann hasn’t yet answered the complaint, and his spokesperson has said only that he’s “exercising the right of authors to reclaim their work and in this case Michael Mann’s original creation.”.

It has been revealed that the strangest thing about this case is that Mann is trying to terminate a grant that, by Latest Regency’s account, nobody can document. Why not the 1994 Warner Bros. agreement, which is in writing?

Recent findings suggest that I can think of a couple of reasons. First, that deal was made by his loan-out, which assigned the screenplay as material Mann wrote for it “as a work made for hire.” Mann signed too, but only to be personally bound “to the extent necessary,” which isn’t the same as granting rights himself. That’s John Waite’s problem all over again. Then there’s the calendar. Even if Mann could terminate the 1994 deal, he couldn’t do it before December 2030. A 1988 grant, on Mann’s reading, gets him there in 2028.

But even if an oral grant can be terminated (New Regency indicates it can’t, because it was never “executed”), what does Mann get back? An exclusive license or transfer of ownership requires a signed writing, so the most ZZY could have received via an oral conversation was a nonexclusive license. New Regency says its exclusive rights come through the 1994 deal, not through ZZY. Ending a nonexclusive license to ZZY wouldn’t touch rights that reached New Regency some other way. So Mann could win the termination fight and still not get back what he actually wants.

The larger prize may come after Heat 2. In July, TheWrap reported that Amazon is already exploring Heat 3, and that the franchise’s long-term value was part of why it took on the sequel. If Mann succeeds in reclaiming rights that New Regency currently controls, he could have real leverage over future Heat projects, while New Regency would keep the 1995 film and whatever was added to the story after those early drafts. Depending on what Mann actually gets back, neither side may be able to make another Heat movie without the other, which would put them in the same spot as Pacino and De Niro at the diner: across a table from each other, with a lot to talk about.

Sources indicate that fresh Regency looks to have a strong case, at least on the facts we have now. But not because Mann supposedly made a deal with himself. Contracting with yourself is the whole business model of a loan-out, and New Regency is the one insisting the court respect Mann’s.

Mann has a plausible answer to the work-for-hire argument. He doesn’t appear to be saying his loan-out was an artifice or should be disregarded, but rather that the work at issue was written outside of it. A court could agree without blowing up anybody’s tax returns. And the work-for-hire labels aren’t conclusive. In August 1994, Mann signed a certificate declaring that everything he had “heretofore or hereafter” written relating to Heat was a work made for hire. But in Marvel Characters, Inc. v. Simon, the Second Circuit held that simply calling a work “made for hire” after the fact doesn’t make it one. So a certificate signed in 1994 isn’t necessarily determinative of what actually happened in 1982.

It has been revealed that the difficulty for Mann is proving it. “Outside my employment” is hard to show when writing was your job. Two years after Simon, the same court held in the Martha Graham case that dances Graham created while employed full-time to choreograph belonged to her employer, however much creative freedom she had.

Sources indicate that and the paper trail here may defeat Mann’s theory in any event. According to New Regency, in the 1989 Ajar agreement, signed less than six months after the supposed oral deal, Mann warranted that the “Hanna” rights hadn’t been transferred to anyone, even though his first notice describes the work he orally assigned as “Heat a/k/a … Hanna.” And while Mann can argue the work-for-hire language was boilerplate, he’ll have to explain why it appears in agreements spanning nearly two decades, some of which he signed twice. (Then there’s the question I raised in 2023: if his best writing fell outside his employment, what exactly was his loan-out getting? The IRS might find that as interesting as a federal judge does.).

Recent findings suggest that even if Mann clears all that, he still has to connect a 1988 oral grant to rights that, by Latest Regency’s account, came through the 1994 deal. The picture could change once Mann answers the complaint and the early drafts surface. Until then, New Regency’s documents beat Mann’s memory.

Robert De Niro’s character in Heat, Neil McCauley, lived by a rule against getting attached to anything he couldn’t walk out on in thirty seconds. Mann has been attached to Heat for fifty years and to his loan-out for just as long, and this case may force him to choose between them.

#324. How to Intercept HTTP/3 Traffic: QUIC and Qpack

📅 25 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2531 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Interceptsuite

How to Intercept HTTP/3 Traffic: QUIC and Qpack

📅 25 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Interceptsuite

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, short answer: HTTP/3 does not go through an HTTP proxy, because it runs over QUIC, and QUIC runs over UDP.
  • It has been revealed that in this post we intercept real HTTP/3 traffic from curl and from Microsoft Edge.
  • Industry observers note that this post uses InterceptSuite, so you should know what it is and what it is not.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, short answer: HTTP/3 does not go through an HTTP proxy, because it runs over QUIC, and QUIC runs over UDP. Most HTTP proxies, such as Burp Suite, are built on HTTP over TCP, so they never see it. To intercept HTTP/3 you need a proxy that can relay UDP and can act as a man in the middle for QUIC. After that, the work is about streams and header compression: the request is not text any more, it is bytes on a QUIC stream, compressed with QPACK.

It has been revealed that in this post we intercept real HTTP/3 traffic from curl and from Microsoft Edge. Then we use a small lab server to look at every byte, so the QUIC and QPACK parts are easy to follow.

Industry observers note that this post uses InterceptSuite, so you should know what it is and what it is not. It is not built for HTTP. It is built for raw network traffic: TCP, TLS, UDP, DTLS and QUIC. Because it can intercept UDP and QUIC, it can handle HTTP/3 too. But it does not come with an HTTP parser, and that is also true for HTTP/3. The core reveals raw bytes.

Recent findings suggest that to read and edit those bytes as HTTP, InterceptSuite has an extension API, and there is an official, open source HTTP/3 extension that decodes the QUIC stream and QPACK headers into text. You can read the code, change it, or send a fix. The decoding in the screenshots below comes from that extension, not from the core.

If you have only used HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, three things are different.

Recent findings suggest that 1. It runs on QUIC, not TCP. HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) is HTTP carried over QUIC (RFC 9000). QUIC packets travel inside UDP datagrams. TLS 1.3 is part of the QUIC handshake (RFC 9001), so there is no separate "TCP then TLS" step.

2. The client has to learn that the server speaks HTTP/3. The ALPN name for HTTP/3 is h3. A server can advertise it with an Alt-Svc response header, and a DNS HTTPS record can advertise it too (RFC 9460). So a browser often makes its first request over TCP, then moves to QUIC.

In a recent development, 3. Everything is a stream. A QUIC connection carries many streams. The two lowest bits of a stream ID tell you what it is (RFC 9000, section 2.1):.

In HTTP/3, every client-started two-way stream is one request and its response (stream 0, 4, 8 and so on). The one-way streams are for housekeeping: a control stream, and two QPACK streams. Their type is the first byte on the stream: 0x00 control, 0x02 QPACK encoder, 0x03 QPACK decoder (RFC 9114, section 6.2 and RFC 9204, section 4.2).

One more detail that matters for interception. The first packets of a QUIC connection (the Initial packets) are protected with keys that anyone can calculate from the connection ID, so they have no real secrecy (RFC 9001, section 5). That is why a passive observer can still see things like the server name in the handshake. Everything after the handshake is encrypted with keys from the TLS 1.3 exchange. You cannot read it without being one of the two ends. A proxy that wants to read HTTP/3 has to be one of the two ends.

HTTP proxies use CONNECT to open a tunnel. In HTTP/3, CONNECT still builds a tunnel to a TCP connection (RFC 9114, section 4.4). To tunnel UDP over HTTP there is a different method, CONNECT-UDP (RFC 9298), and most tools and apps do not use it.

In a recent development, SOCKS5 can relay UDP. The command is UDP ASSOCIATE (RFC 1928). But many clients never use it. For example, the Chromium network docs say that in Chrome, SOCKSv5 is only used to proxy TCP-based requests and cannot relay UDP (Chromium proxy docs). So pointing a browser at a SOCKS5 proxy does not send its QUIC traffic through that proxy, and you are not testing the QUIC path.

That leaves two practical ways to get QUIC traffic into a proxy:.

For how this compares with mitmproxy, see the QUIC interception post.

Open Proxy, then Redirect, click Add, type the program name (for example curl.exe), leave the action on Proxy, and save. Then click Start Redirect. The status line claims Redirecting through the proxy at 127.0.0.1:4444, and the program's TCP and UDP traffic goes through InterceptSuite without changing any setting in the program.

Industry observers note that A rule can also limit the destination hosts and ports. The first matching rule decides, and programs that match no rule are left alone. Remember to trust the InterceptSuite CA on the machine, as in the quick start.

curl is a good first test because it is simple and does exactly what you tell it. It needs a build with HTTP/3 support. This example runs on Windows. The curl that ships with Windows (8.21.0 here) does not support HTTP/3: curl -V does not list HTTP3 in its features. So we installed a second curl build that does:.

The fresh build (8.23.0) lists HTTP3, ngtcp2 and nghttp3 in curl -V. Check yours the same way before you test, and make sure the new curl is the one that runs (open a new terminal after the install).

Recent findings suggest that --http3-only makes curl use HTTP/3 and nothing else, so it cannot quietly fall back to TCP. With the Redirect rule on, curl worked without any proxy option and its output revealed HTTP/3 200. No -k was needed, because curl used the Windows trust store, where the InterceptSuite CA is installed.

In Proxy History the connection appeared as QUIC with host cloudflare-quic.com and ALPN h3:.

The first client packet (46 bytes) is the request. With the HTTP/3 tab it reads like this:.

Now turn Intercept ON, run curl again, and change the request while it is held. Replace user-agent: curl/8.23.0 with user-agent: edited-by-proxy and press Forward:.

According to recent reports, the test site prints back what it saw. The first run notes uag=curl/8.23.0. The run with the edit says:.

So the server got the edited header, and curl never knew. The response is readable too:.

Look at curl's SETTINGS frame, from the client:.

According to recent reports, QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY: 0 means curl does not use the QPACK dynamic table at all. That is why every curl request is easy to read and edit. We will see the opposite case later.

Browsers are harder, for two reasons.

The fix is to start the browser with three flags:.

It has been revealed that is the base64 SHA-256 of the CA's public key. You calculate it from your own CA file:.

Industry observers note that edge indicates a bar saying the flag is unsupported. That is expected, and it is why you should use a test profile and not your daily one. Close all Edge windows before you start it, or the flags are ignored.

With the Redirect rule for msedge.exe on, open https://cloudflare-quic.com/. The page states "your browser used HTTP/3":.

According to recent reports, in InterceptSuite the same visit was a QUIC connection with ALPN h3. The request from Edge, decoded by the extension:.

And the response, with the alt-svc: h3=":443" header the site uses to advertise HTTP/3:.

The response body here is content-encoding: gzip. The extension decompresses it for display, so the body reveals as HTML.

Edge's SETTINGS are very different from curl's:.

Sources indicate that edge offers a 64 KB dynamic table and up to 100 blocked streams, so after the first request, Edge can send headers as table references. The QPACK section below explains what that means for reading and editing.

UDP ASSOCIATE works in two parts.

The header, from RFC 1928 section 7:.

The association lives as long as the TCP connection that asked for it. If that TCP connection closes, the UDP association ends (RFC 1928, section 6). This is easy to forget when you write your own client.

Recent findings suggest that interceptSuite listens on 127.0.0.1:4444 for SOCKS5 over TCP and 127.0.0.1:4445 for the UDP relay (see the quick start). The reply to UDP ASSOCIATE points to 127.0.0.1:4445.

Real servers make it hard to see what is going on, so here is a small lab. Both sides use Python and aioquic.

The lab client skips certificate checks. That is fine for a lab. A real app must trust the proxy's CA certificate, or it will close the connection when it sees the forged certificate. See Install the CA certificate for that step.

The lab client sent one request:.

Here is Proxy History after the client connected, sent requests, and closed.

Industry observers note that the host column demonstrates h3.lab.test. That is the server name from the TLS handshake. The ALPN column shows h3. The Protocol column says QUIC.

Industry observers note that the thing most people do not expect is the number of rows. One request gave 10 entries, not 2. Each row is a chunk of data from one QUIC stream, in the order the proxy saw it. The small ones are all HTTP/3 housekeeping:.

The client's control stream is three bytes longer than the server's: 0D 01 08 at the end, which is a MAX_PUSH_ID frame.

According to recent reports, filtering helps a lot here. The filter box understands things like connection_id == 3 and size > 100. The available fields are src_ip, dst_ip, port, direction, protocol, size, modified, connection_id, type, data, host and alpn.

With the HTTP/3 extension loaded, the control stream entry is shown as text:.

According to recent reports, the 50 00 part is a QUIC variable-length integer. The first two bits (01) say it uses two bytes, and the value is 0x1000, which is 4096. This one matters later, because QPACK's dynamic table is off by default. Both QPACK settings default to zero (RFC 9204, section 5). This server turned it on and allowed 16 blocked streams.

Sources indicate that now the request itself. This is the raw view of the held request packet:.

According to recent reports, you can see the body (user=alice&pw=hunter2), because the body is not compressed. The headers are unreadable. This is QPACK. It is HPACK's cousin for HTTP/3 (RFC 9204), and it does three things:.

The HTTP/3 extension from the Extension repository decodes all of this into text. Open the HTTP/3 tab on the same packet:.

Industry observers note that the core of InterceptSuite shows HTTP/3 as raw bytes. The decoded view comes from this extension. The extension is a normal Python file, and you can read it. Its _decode function parses the QUIC variable-length integers, the HTTP/3 frames, then the QPACK block with the static table and Huffman decoder.

According to recent reports, turn Intercept ON. By default it holds client-to-server packets. There is also an Intercept response option for the other direction.

Recent findings suggest that when the client sends its request, the request packet is held and the queue states 1 packet(s) waiting. Change two things in the HTTP/3 tab: the x-demo header and the body.

Sources indicate that then press Forward. The server printed this:.

Recent findings suggest that so the server received the edited request. The client got a normal 200 answer from the server, and its own copy of the request was never changed.

In Proxy History, the row shows Modified: Yes, and the viewer can show the Original and Edited versions:.

Two practical points from doing this:.

The extension does not patch the old bytes. It builds a upcoming HEADERS frame. From the source, the rules are:.

This is the part that needs care. So far everything decoded nicely. Now send more requests on the same connection (same headers, different path) and look again.

The sizes tell the story. Requests 1 and 2 were 122 bytes each. Request 3 was 13 bytes. And at some point, a 114-byte entry indicated up on the client's QPACK encoder stream.

Here are the 13 bytes of request 3, the way they were on the wire:.

Recent findings suggest that where are the entries? In the 114-byte entry on the encoder stream. Its first bytes are C0 88 9D 95 E8 1C 6B A4 A8 4F, which is "insert :authority, with a Huffman-coded value" (the value decodes to h3.lab.test). The client sent the long header values once, and every later request only sends numbers. This is a good design. It is also what makes interception harder.

Look at what the HTTP/3 tab shows for request 3:.

The server's response did the same thing. After a few responses, its header block started using the dynamic table, and the HTTP/3 tab highlights the body but only placeholders for two of the headers:.

There is one more thing to see here. In the capture, the 13-byte request (row 30) arrived before the 114-byte encoder stream entry (row 31). That is allowed by design. QPACK lets a request stream wait ("block") until the inserts it needs have arrived. The server declared it could keep up to 16 blocked streams (the QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS setting we saw above). Later a single byte 88 comes back from the server on its decoder stream. That is a Section Acknowledgment for stream 8, which was the third request: the decoder tells the encoder it processed a header block that needed the table (RFC 9204, section 4.4.1).

So two things follow for a tester:.

Right-click a row in Proxy History and choose Send to Replay.

The session opens with the details filled in: host, port, protocol QUIC, ALPN h3, Newly introduced bidirectional stream, and End stream (FIN) ticked. HTTP/3 request streams are client-started two-way streams, so that is the correct choice. The FIN flag matters because the lab server only answers after it sees the end of the request.

In the lab the host name h3.lab.test is only a name in the TLS handshake and does not resolve, so change the host to 127.0.0.1. In the HTTP/3 tab, change the path to /admin and x-demo to replayed, then press Send.

The conversation highlights what happened on the wire:.

The server printed GET /admin x-demo= replayed, and the response JSON reveals "path": "/admin" and "x_demo": "replayed".

If the edited text leaves a broken header block, Replay sends only a few bytes (25 here) and the server closes the connection:.

Sources indicate that 0x106 is H3_FRAME_ERROR. RFC 9114 states that if a stream ends and the last frame on it is cut short, the receiver must treat it as a connection error of this type (RFC 9114, section 7.1). In plain words: the frame header promised more bytes than the stream delivered. If you hand-craft HTTP/3 bytes in the Raw or Hex tab, this is the error you will meet first. It means your frame length does not match your data.

You can find the current list in the protocol compatibility matrix.

Related reading: Replay documentation, Proxy History documentation, the HTTP/3 extension source, and Intercepting QUIC and HTTP/3 when mitmproxy isn't enough.
